#1103. Hideki Shirakawa obituary: chemist who showed that plastics can conduct electricity

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Kazuo Akagi is a research professor at Ritsumeikan University, Kusatsu, Japan, and professor emeritus at Kyoto University and the University of Tsukuba. He worked with Shirakawa on polyacetylene thin films starting in 1984, when he joined Shirakawa’s lab at the University of Tsukuba.

Hideki Shirakawa pioneered the field of conductive polymers, overturning the common view that plastics do not conduct electricity. His demonstration that thin films of polyacetylene — an organic polymer — can become conductive when doped with small amounts of other chemicals earned him a share of the 2000 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (with Alan MacDiarmid and Alan Heeger). He was the second Japanese chemist to receive this award, after Kenichi Fukui in 1981. Shirakawa has died aged 90.

Shirakawa was born in Tokyo. After graduating from secondary school in Takayama City, he studied chemical engineering at the Tokyo Institute of Technology (now the Institute of Science Tokyo). He went on to pursue master’s and doctoral studies there, under the supervision of polymer chemist Shu Kambara, earning a Doctor of Engineering degree for his research on how blocks of organic molecules combine to form polymer chains.

Chemistry education must change to help the planet: here’s how

Chemistry education must change to help the planet: here’s how

After completing his doctorate in 1966, Shirakawa was hired as a research associate in the laboratory of Sakuji Ikeda at Tokyo Tech. There, he began studying how acetylene molecules join together to form a polymer, using Ziegler–Natta catalysts (which are based on organic molecules containing transition metals).

In 1967, Shirakawa was joined in his experiments by a visiting researcher from South Korea, Hyung Chick Pyun. The pair were polymerizing acetylene using a catalyst composed of tetrabutoxytitanium and triethylaluminium to produce powdered polyacetylene.

On one occasion, however, the protocol failed to produce the powder. Instead, a ragged film formed on the surface of the solution in the flask. On closer inspection, it became clear that the visiting researcher had mistakenly used a much higher concentration of the catalyst than was intended — 1,000 times higher. Shirakawa went on to synthesize a thin film of polyacetylene with a metallic lustre by introducing acetylene gas into a flask coated on the inside with the concentrated catalyst.

Chemists struggle to ditch hazardous solvents — even after decades of ‘green’ efforts

Chemists struggle to ditch hazardous solvents — even after decades of ‘green’ efforts

Subsequently, he travelled to the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, where he worked with MacDiarmid and Heeger. The team discovered that adding small amounts of molecules that accept electrons (such as bromine) or that donate electrons (such as arsenic pentafluoride) increased the electrical conductivity of the thin film by a factor of ten million. This work led to the trio’s Nobel award.

The Argentine, who took the reigns of the US national side on a contract running through until 2030, recounted how the most successful manager in British history once sought him out.

#1095. Liverpool calamity hands Iraola his most chastening night yet

Andoni Iraola looked up to the ceiling of Fenerbahce’s media auditorium as he tried to find the words to describe the madness he had just witnessed.

“Cheap” was his first conclusion, swiftly followed by “messy”; technically, Liverpool’s head coach was right but this was a moment when nobody would have found issue had he gone further. “Absurd” and “preposterous” would have been more accurate portrayals of this calamity.

Liverpool have won two European trophies in Istanbul, but they do not tend to enjoy visits to Turkey. Roy Hodgson, in August 2010, was the last Anfield manager to oversee a win here and there was an irony that the hero of that night in Trabzon – Dirk Kuyt – masterminded this downfall.

Kuyt, interim head coach, got a remarkable response out of a Fenerbahce team who had amassed 1,086 Premier League appearances between them and he was as giddy as the locals after Mason Greenwood, Archie Brown and substitute Vedat Muriqi scored to give the club a famous night.

Another quickfire equaliser for Fenerbahçe 💨 Archie Brown brings the Turkish side level ⚽️ 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/8kZUXPEC3C

But even Kuyt would have been the first to recognise the helping hand Fenerbahce were afforded. Liverpool were meek, naïve, and while the Turkish side danced in the rain on the Asian side of the city, Iraola was left to dissect the most chastening 90 minutes of his short Anfield career.

“It’s frustration because it’s a difficult place to come here and to play,” said Iraola. “During most of the game, we were thinking: ‘OK we can win this one.’ But obviously it hasn’t happened. We conceded, I think, messy goals, especially the first and the third one. The second one is a rebound.”

Yet it all started so smoothly. For all that Fenerbahce tried to put Liverpool out of their stride with a soundtrack of high-pitched whistling, Iraola’s side kept the ball well and they might have been ahead in the fifth minute but Victor Muñoz and Bradley Barcola, playing as a central striker, erred.

Another chance went begging when Joe Gomez fizzed a ball across the six-yard box that was screaming to be converted, but nobody could apply the finishing touch. When Trey Nyoni put Liverpool ahead, it seemed like all those local predictions of a resounding away win would come true.

Since Manchester United felt duty-bound to sell Greenwood in 2024 the former England forward has continued his career away from the Premier League. After leaving Marseille he has found a home in Istanbul where the fans have taken to him and they bellowed his name following the equaliser.

One added minute at the end of this first half.

Greenwood has been Fenerbahce’s best player by far tonight and he tests Alisson. Lukaku finds Greenwood with a pass forward down the left channel and, from inside the Liverpool penalty area, the latter forces Alisson into a decent save.

What started off as an encouraging performance has descended into something ordinary at best for Liverpool. They are being overrun in midfield and the pace of Greenwood down Fenerbahce’s right has the beating of Kostas Tsimikas on every occasion. Andoni Iraola will be delighted to get in for half-time all square - if Liverpool can see it out.

Greenwood has an opportunity from the right side of the box. He tries to beat Alisson at his near post but drags it wide.

Munoz’s cross from near the byline is met by Barcola and the Frenchman’s header goes narrowly wide of the far post.

Mason Greenwood is having his name bellowed around the stadium though the deflection off Jeremy Jacquet is the only reason he has scored. The visitors take the lead in Istanbul and it is 19-year-old Nyoni who scores. A cross from Szoboszlai into the Fenerbahce penalty area is headed out to the edge of the box, where Nyoni volleys it first time. The shot takes a small deflection off Oppong and beats Ederson.

Andoni Iraola says he will not waste any more time thinking about the penalty Liverpool were denied against Arsenal and won’t seek an explanation from Pro Ref. There was a significant fallout following the 1-0 loss at Anfield on Sunday with many judges believing Stuart Attwell, who was VAR, should have consulted match official Andy Madley to highlight an obvious pull by Jurrien Timber that prevented Alexander Isak heading a Bradley Barcola cross.

Liverpool’s head coach explained in the heat of the moment that he would tell his players to go down if they felt contact in the area and Cody Gakpo, the Netherlands international, explained last night in Istanbul it was a message the squad had taken on board.

“As a team, we play pretty fair – maybe we should dive some more like the gaffer said,” Gakpo, who also had claims to be awarded a penalty against Arsenal, explained. “On both occasions you could have given a penalty or a foul, but they decided not. We have to live with the decision. That’s it.”

But as angry as he was with the situation, Iraola has drawn a line on the matter. He is not going to seek out Pro Ref for a discussion – even though he feels a number of decisions have gone against Liverpool this season – and is channelling his energy into other situations.

Iraola said: “I didn’t ask for an explanation and I haven’t received an explanation, no. I told you what you I think about the plays but, honestly, I don’t have the time to [speak to Pro Ref]. I have been preparing for Fenerbahce. It is just two days between games so I have just been focusing on this game and the opposition and how to prepare the team.”

Liverpool have made the long trip to Turkey to take on Fenerbahce on matchday four of the Champions League.

Liverpool enter this fixture having won all three Champions League matches thus far, beating Atletico Madrid, LASK and Villarreal to make it nine points from nine for Andoni Iraola’s side. Liverpool’s five-game unbeaten streak was ended by Arsenal in the league on Sunday. They return to the city where the club enjoyed one of their most memorable nights, beating AC Milan in the Champions League final 21 years ago.

“Istanbul is always going to be very special for Liverpool,” Iraola said. “It is difficult to find a more important night. Tomorrow [tonight] it won’t be easy, you talk about statistics, especially English teams playing here. They have very good players and a very good squad, they know how to play in this competition. We have to start strong in the game. It is very early in the season to establish comparisons. We want to continue how we have done in the Champions League, three games and nine points, it is a good chance to get to 12 points and then finish in the top eight. Champions League away is very difficult.”

In addition to the long-term absentees Hugo Ekitike, Conor Bradley and Giovanni, both Ryan Gravenberch and Jeremie Frimpong have missed the trip to Turkey.

Fenerbahce have made a slow start to their Champions League campaign, taking just two points from their opening three fixtures. They have drawn twice against Roma and Slavia Prague at home whilst they suffered a heavy 6-0 loss at Aston Villa. Former Liverpool forward Dirk Kuyt has been appointed their interim coach following the resignation of Ismail Kartal following their recent defeat to arch rivals Galatasaray just over a week ago.

“It is a great opportunity for us to show what we can do,” Kuyt said. “It is also a great opportunity for me, a game between two teams that are very important to me. We have a very good plan, and we have to believe in this plan. No-one who loves Fenerbahce is happy with the current situation, but this is a huge opportunity. We have players who have won the Champions League and the World Cup.”

They come into tonight’s match having lost back-to-back league games since drawing against Slavia Prague on matchday three of the Champions League. They have plenty of former Premier League players in their ranks, including Ederson, N’Golo Kante and Romelu Lukaku.

Kevin De Bruyne to Everton is on, with the Manchester City legend struggling at Napoli

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Everton have launched a shock bid for former Manchester City man, Kevin De Bruyne.

The Belgian is a legend of the Premier League, having won six titles and racked up an in while racking up almost 200 goal involvements in 288 appearances in the English top flight – but since leaving the Etihad, things haven't been as rosy for him in Italian football.

Now, Everton are prepared to offer the 35-year-old a return to the northwest of England in one of the biggest-name moves of the Toffees' recent history.

De Bruyne spent 10 years at Manchester City before swapping one blue shirt for another and signing for Napoli last summer.

The playmaker has struggled to make a difference in Serie A, however, with Calciomercato reporting that he “appears to be in a decline mentally and could sensationally return to the Premier League in January.”

The report notes that Everton are making a sensational swoop to bring De Bruyne back to England and have already made contact with the player's entourage.

The Merseysiders are up to sixth in the Premier League at the moment and enjoying a good season, despite leaving themselves short over the summer in terms of transfer business.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Fans were disappointed when the club sold striker Beto without a replacement – leaving Thierno Barry as the only recognised No.9 at the Hill Dickinson Stadium – while a failure to replace long-serving right-back Seamus Coleman after his retirement has meant that midfielder Merlin Rohl has taken the role on this term.

There has been recent uncertainty regarding the loan spell of Jack Grealish, too, with the England international dropped by manager David Moyes after breaching the club's disciplinary rules when he reportedly skipped training.

Grealish – who is on loan from Man City, incidentally – has very little chance of joining the Toffees permanently now, with some suggesting that his loan spell could be curtailed in January.

De Bruyne's contract runs until 2027, with the Partenopei holding an option for another year.

Whether club president Aurelio De Laurentiis decides to release the player midseason remains another matter.

The 35-year-old is worth €8 million, as per Transfermarkt. Everton travel away to Brentford when Premier League action resumes after the international break.

#1093. How I balance my life as a professional surfer and a university researcher

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Cliff Kapono is a professional surfer and marine conservation scientist.

Cliff Kapono enjoys professional surfing as an adjunct to his academic career. Credit: Nani Welch Keliihoomalu for Nature

During my graduate studies at the University of California, San Diego, long hours in the laboratory were often stressful, and not just because of the research. Most of my anxiety came from looking out the window at perfect surfing conditions and realizing I didn’t have much time to finish my experiments and leave while the ‘waves were firing’.

Several years on, I am now an assistant professor at the School of Ocean Futures at Arizona State University (ASU), working from Hilo, Hawaii, where I balance scientific research with my second job: travelling the world as a non-competitive professional surfer. Also known as a free surfer, I ride a variety of board designs — from conventional wooden surfboards to modern big-wave ‘guns’ — and produce social-media content, such as photos and videos, in exchange for endorsement opportunities.

My research is also deeply connected to the ocean. I study coral microbiomes, sampling the community of microorganisms living on and in the coral before and after environmental stress to improve understanding of reef health and the sea-bed formations that create waves, referred to as surf breaks. In May, my colleagues and I reported on the importance of creating a framework to analyse systems with environmental, social and cultural components to protect surf ecosystems1.

In my faculty position, I work in nine-month appointments, and I am permitted to spend a number of work hours each calendar year on non-conflicting outside business. I spend roughly 85% of my work year on research and teaching and 15% on surfing assignments.

Many careers are no longer confined to a single discipline or identity, and some of the most meaningful work now happens at the intersection between different skills, communities and ways of thinking. Surfing shapes the questions I want to ask as a scientist, while science provides me with ways to understand and protect ocean environments. When I was a student, I used to worry that I would have to choose between surfing and science. Today, my career exists because I didn’t.

When I graduated from high school in 2005, Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders made up less than 0.2% of all science, technology, engineering and mathematics degree graduates in the United States. Today, that number remains at only 0.3%2. As a Native Hawaiian kid, targeted fellowships and private programmes made university possible for me, covering my tuition and board.

After I started a PhD chemistry programme at the University of California, San Diego, in 2012, my studies became much more demanding. Courses, a teaching-assistant role, fellowship requirements and lab training would keep me on land from sunrise until sundown. Despite being able to see the ocean from nearly every window on campus, it was the time in my life that I felt furthest from it.

Remarkably, it was during the third year of my PhD programme that getting paid to surf actually became a reality. After many nights spent in the lab, I decided to set academic boundaries and rededicate time to the waves, mostly as a way to protect my mental health. I stopped measuring success only by hours in the lab. Instead, I treated time in the ocean as part of the scientific process.

Can a 'lullaby' save coral reefs from extinction?

Can a 'lullaby' save coral reefs from extinction?

Surfing-industry figures took notice, and not long after becoming more present on the beaches, I was offered modest ambassadorial contracts that developed into respectable budgets that let me travel to places with better waves and to collaborate with local board builders — when not in the lab, of course.

When I moved back to Hawaii in 2018, I received a US National Science Foundation postdoctoral fellowship for broadening participation of under-represented groups in biology and I began to use surfing as a vehicle for communicating coral science. That eventually led to Arizona State University recruiting me to join its Hilo-based Center for Global Discovery and Conservation Science in 2021, a position that has since evolved into my current role.

Blending the two disciplines has made my research more creative and my surfing more meaningful. It also taught me the importance of protecting time for the parts of life that keep you grounded. Whether that be surfing, music, art or family, maintaining space for your passions is not a distraction from academic work; it is often the very thing that sustains it.

Here are some guiding principles that have helped me to navigate the worlds of surfing and academia.

The best experiences come when you find a crew that wants to surf the same waves or explore the same questions as you. Some of the most important opportunities in my career came from relationships that started organically, often through time spent in the ocean and local communities, or through a shared curiosity, rather than formal networking.

The researchers, surfers, photographers and conservationists I work with are people who genuinely care about the places we study and the communities connected to them. Over time, those shared values create trust that later opens doors to research projects, publications, funding opportunities and creative collaborations. I’ve found that the best way to find these people is not by chasing status or connections but by consistently showing up in the communities and places that you genuinely care about.

#1091. Mauricio Pochettino faces nightmare Man United start as it emerges he WILL take charge of USA game in early hours of Wednesday - cutting preparation time for debut trip to Liverpool

Published: 10:58 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 18:11 EST, 12 November 2026

Mauricio Pochettino will face a brutal start to life at Manchester United with the prospective Red Devils boss set to manage the United States days before his debut at Liverpool.

United have moved closer to putting Pochettino in charge at Old Trafford after reaching a verbal agreement with the US national team boss on Wednesday. The club then made a formal approach to US Soccer. He will reportedly sign a two-and-a-half-year deal.

Daily Mail Sport understands Pochettino will take charge of both of the United States matches during the international window.

The US take on Haiti in the CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final first leg on Saturday, with the second fixture then taking place in Cincinnati on Tuesday evening, but would likely finish at around 2am GMT.

Pochettino would then have to travel to Manchester following the match to link up with the Red Devils' squad for the first time, likely on Thursday.

The Argentine would then have limited time with his players before a daunting trip to Anfield to face rivals Liverpool on Sunday in a blockbuster first match in charge.

Mauricio Pochettino will take charge of the United States upcoming matches against Haiti

Pochettino will coach in the early hours on Wednesday morning in Cincinnati before travelling to Manchester

The Argentine would have limited time to prepare his side for Sunday's match at Anfield

Man United are said to be relaxed over Pochettino taking charge of his final two matches as US boss before starting as their new head coach.

It will cost Pochettino around £7million to buy himself out of his contract with the US Soccer Federation, with United ready to foot the bill.

The cost of bringing in his back-room team, including trusted assistants Jesus Perez and Miguel D’Agostino, will take the cost above £10million.

The 54-year-old only signed a new deal after the World Cup meaning that United could have got him for nothing in the summer.

Pochettino is set to take over a Man United side languishing in the Premier League relegation zone following just one win in their opening ten matches.

The trip to Anfield would be the first of a run of eight matches in 29 days, as Man United juggle Premier League and Champions League football.

Pochettino is set to succeed Michael Carrick, whose departure as the Red Devils' boss was officially announced on Wednesday morning.

Pochettino will face a tight turnaround to prepare his new side for the daunting clash on Merseyside

Carrick arrived at United's training ground at 7.50am this morning and was dismissed. He left at 10.18am, less than two and a half hours later. He is the first Premier League manager to be sacked this season, followed hours later by bottom-of-the-table Crystal Palace boss Pierre Sage.

In a statement released at 10.37am, Carrick's sacking was confirmed. United's statement read: 'After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions.

'Michael is, and always will be, a Manchester United legend. Just as he did as a player, he has conducted himself with the highest standards of dedication and professionalism throughout his time back with the club. His leadership and achievements last season will always be fondly remembered.'

Carrick's backroom team have also left the club with Pochettino set to bring his own staff to United.

Assistant boss Steve Holland, coaches Jonathan Woodgate, Jonny Evans and Travis Binnion, and goalkeeping coach Craig Mawson have all gone, although United didn't initially confirm the news because not all of them were at the training ground this morning and had to be told in person.

#1089. Gyokeres the creator and executioner to see nervous Arsenal past Slavia Prague

With a stylish assist and a gorgeous goal, Viktor Gyokeres produced the sort of match-winning performance that suggests the Swedish striker is making significant progress at last. It has not always been straightforward for him at Arsenal, but this was unquestionably one of his better showings, and it continued an encouraging upturn in his form.

Gyokeres has been the second-choice striker for most of this season, with Mikel Arteta usually preferring the more subtle Kai Havertz in attack. There are signs, though, that Gyokeres is now growing in belief. Following this victory over Slavia Prague, which was much more narrow and nervy than it should have been, he has now scored two goals and registered three assists in his last five appearances.

Even more promising than those statistics was his all-round play in Prague. In the first half especially, Gyokeres held on to long passes, combined with his team-mates and tested the opposition with his runs in behind. For Arsenal’s first goal, he found Noni Madueke with a brilliant pass. For their second, he curled a fabulous strike into the top corner.

What a finish from Viktor Gyökeres from a tight angle 📐🎯 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/EET5P7aJ2X

“Really good,” said Arteta of Gyokeres. “Not only the assist and the goal, but he was really connected to the team. It’s great news, because I think he needed that performance.”

Those two moments in the first half eventually ensured another European victory for Arteta’s side, but the manager was far from impressed with the second-half showing. So smooth at first, Arsenal became remarkably ragged by the end. Slavia were deserving of their goal, scored by Wiktor Nowak. It looked like complacency had infected the minds of the Arsenal players, and you could feel Arteta’s fury radiating from the touchline.

“We scored two goals and it should have been three, four or five,” said Arteta. “And at half-time the message was clear: there is still a lot to do in this game. Right from the beginning of the second half, we were extremely far from our standards in everything that we have to do, in every basic, in every concept, and in everything we discussed. So much to improve and I take full responsibility for that.”

Without Gabriel Magalhães and David Raya, who both made dramatic stops on the goal-line, this could have become an ugly night for Arsenal against one of the weaker teams in the Champions League. The Czech side have now gone 23 games without a victory in Europe’s premier competition, which equals the longest winless run in European Cup history.

It was a remarkable coincidence that this game fell on November 4, the exact date as the same fixture last season. On that occasion Arsenal were comfortable 3-0 winners, with Mikel Merino scoring twice, and they seemed to be heading towards a similar night when Madueke scored the early opener.

The goal was made by Gyokeres, who held off a defender and then hooked an excellent pass into Madueke’s path. The Arsenal winger had already established his dominance over Oskar Kubiak, his opposite number, and he reached fifth gear before the Polish defender had even reached second. Madueke then slid his finish beneath the body of Nazar Domchak, Slavia’s teenage goalkeeper.

A fantastic pass from Gyökeres and a lovely finish from Madueke 🪄 The Arsenal attackers combine to great effect 🤝 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/blmMILZxok

Just as Gyokeres is finding his form, so is Madueke. The absence of the injured Bukayo Saka has given Madueke a run in the side and he seems to be benefiting from it, even if he still lacks the same consistency in decision-making as his England team-mate.

One of Slavia’s many problems in a one-sided first half was their inability to cope with Arsenal’s rotations in midfield. Declan Rice, Martín Zubimendi and Merino were all alternating positions at will, taking turns to drop deep and push forward. Merino could have scored a couple, before he combined sharply with Gyokeres for Arsenal’s second.

Gyokeres has never been the most delicate link-up player, and there have been too many times when the ball has simply bounced off him, but here he was impressively sleek. A quick exchange of passes with Merino allowed him a sight of goal, and the curled finish was sumptuous. For a man known for his power, this was an uncharacteristic demonstration of finesse.

Game over? Arsenal clearly thought so. They certainly came out for the second half like a team that believed the job was done. Arteta became increasingly irate in the first few minutes after the restart, with Ben White on the receiving end of one verbal slap. Rice also received a telling-off, and a yellow card, from the referee after kicking the ball away in annoyance.

Would Slavia have secured a draw if they had been at full strength? They had been weakened by the banishment of their star striker from the club because of a series of disciplinary failings. Tomás Chory, the top scorer for the past two seasons, was chucked out of the team after showing his middle finger to the referee in a recent game. This sort of sanction would have earned Arteta’s approval, no doubt, but it did not increase Slavia’s chances of hurting the Premier League champions in those edgy final few minutes.

Perhaps they will reflect on that decision differently now, given the uncharacteristically wobbly second-half performance by Arsenal. The visitors were vulnerable in the latter stages, when they lacked the control and composure that Arteta expects. Gabriel, too, appeared dismayed by what he was seeing. At one point, he put his hands on his hips and scowled at his team-mates like an angry teacher.

With only a few minutes remaining, Nowak converted a left-wing cross to plunge Arsenal into a proper panic. It required a backs-to-the-wall defensive action, similar to the victory against Liverpool on Sunday, to get over the line.

Always we need to value winning away in the Champions League. It is extremely difficult. Two very different halves. We should have had three or four goals in the first half but we didn’t do it. Right at the start of the second half we were on the back foot, very sloppy and gave balls away. Then we had to suffer. A lot to learn.

We should have scored more in the first half and if we didn’t do that we had to go and do that in the second half.

We made six changes but we know the quality of the players we have. Whether we were lacking something I don’t know but I would have done the same thing [again].

I value what the team has done now, it is 11 away games we played, but our standards should be higher.

Arteta on Gyokeres: "He was really good. A game we believed was good for him, for the spaces he could use. He was really connected to the team. Great news because I think he needed that. Really pleased."

Arteta: "Two very different halves. The first we played at a really high level. At half-time the message was clear: there is still a lot to do in this game. Right from the beginning we were extremely far from our standards. Very far from the standards we expect from each other."

First half we played really, really well. We created a lot of chances and could have scored more but the second half was completely different. They stepped up a gear and made it difficult for us and we have to learn from it. Delighted with the win but a lot of things to improve going forward.

Maybe they started pressing a bit higher with more intensity. We had too many giveaways especially in the final third. There was too much running from box to box and we have to manage those reactions and go for the third and fourth goal.

At the end of the day it is three points.

Slavia Prague managed just one shot on goal in the first half worth 0.12 xG but finished the game with 18 shots on Arsenal’s goal and 2.23 xG. Arsenal could easily have dropped points on the balance of the second 45 minutes.

Quite surprised Declan Rice stayed on the pitch for the full 90 minutes there. He seemed to be in a bit of discomfort after a couple of long sprints. And then he got the silly yellow. Arteta perhaps panicking about the result.

Mosquera with a strong recovery run to defend against Ayaosi in the corner at the expense of a throw-in. It feels like Arsenal are through their rough patch at the start of the half, but Arteta will want the third.

Rice with a chance to pick out Madueke on the counter but his diagonal pass was cut out. Slavia have been sent out with a flea in their ear, and have been much improved so far. Arteta will want Arsenal to stay serious and weather this spell.

Declan Rice is throwing a blanket over any flickering embers of a Slavia Prague attack, and then he is running the game from there. Arsenal’s captain on the night has been imperious so far.

Knockout spots, relegation dogfights, and crucial seeding: why this week's Nations League action matters far more than you think

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Forget the notion of glorified friendlies, this month quarter-final berths, relegation peril, and major tournament seeding is all on the line in the UEFA Nations League.

The final round of group fixtures is anything but an international break distraction.

Here, we break down what it all means for the home nations.

The top two finishers in each League A group advance to a two-legged quarter-final stage, rather than just the group winners qualifying directly for a final-four tournament, as has previously been the case.

This week’s fixtures decide which nations book their place in the knockout bracket to compete for the trophy, while also dictating important top-seed status for the subsequent knockout draw.

The margins between tiers carry significant weight. Finishing top of the group in Leagues B, C, and D earns automatic promotion to the tier above, while finishing bottom of Leagues A, B, and C results in automatic relegation.

Crucially, the introduction of two-legged promotion/relegation play-offs - which will pit third-placed teams in League A against runners-up from League B, and third-placed teams in League B against runners-up from League C - means almost every matchday result directly determines either immediate survival, a climb up the ladder, or a drop into lower-tier fixtures.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Nations League standings double as an insurance policy for future European Championship and FIFA World Cup cycles.

Overall tournament rankings determine the seeding pots for upcoming European qualifying draws, directly affecting the difficulty of qualification paths. The highest-ranked Nations League group winners who fail to secure qualification through standard qualifying groups are handed secondary lifelines via tournament play-off berths.

England currently sit second in their group with nine points, trailing Spain (12 points) but comfortably ahead of Croatia (3 points) and Czechia (0 points).

Because the top two teams in League A advance, Thomas Tuchel's side have already effectively secured their quarter-final berth. The focus now shifts to whether they can overtake Spain for the group's top seed.

Thursday, Nov 12: vs Croatia (H – Wembley Stadium, London) - 19:45 GMT

Sunday, Nov 15: vs Spain (A – Metropolitano Stadium, Madrid) - 19:45 GMT

Wales are third in their top-tier group, trailing Portugal and Denmark, but sitting just above Norway. To avoid a relegation play-off against a League B runner-up or automatic relegation if they drop to fourth, they need results this week to either secure their safety or mount a late push into the top two for a quarter-final spot.

Saturday, Nov 14: vs Norway (A – Ullevaal Stadium, Oslo) - 17:00 GMT

Tuesday, Nov 17: vs Portugal (H – Cardiff City Stadium, Cardiff) - 19:45 GMT

Scotland find themselves in third place behind Switzerland and Slovenia, with North Macedonia rooted to the bottom. Finishing third in League B leads to a relegation play-off against a League C side, so the Tartan Army will be keen to pick up points and push for second place (promotion play-off) or even top spot (automatic promotion).

Friday, Nov 13: vs North Macedonia (H – Hampden Park, Glasgow) - 19:45 GMT

Monday, Nov 16: vs Switzerland (A – Kybunpark, St. Gallen) - 19:45 GMT

Michael O'Neill's side are in an excellent position, currently top of their group ahead of Hungary, Ukraine, and Georgia. If they maintain their first-place standing over the next two games, they will earn automatic promotion to League A.

Saturday, Nov 14: vs Ukraine (H – Windsor Park, Belfast) - 19:45 GMT

Tuesday, Nov 17: vs Hungary (A – Puskas Arena, Budapest) - 19:45 GMT

The Republic of Ireland sit in third on five points, trailing group leaders Austria and second-placed Kosovo. They will need strong performances in this window to climb into the top two for a shot at promotion, or risk facing a relegation play-off to retain their League B status.

Saturday, Nov 14: vs Austria (A – Raiffeisen Arena, Linz) - 19:45 GMT

Tuesday, Nov 17: vs Kosovo (H – Aviva Stadium, Dublin) - 19:45 GMT

England players aired “strong views” in the wake of the World Cup 2026 collapse at the hands of Argentina.

That's according to a report that states says that arguably the Three Lions' two best players, Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham, have been particularly strong in expressing their opinions over the defeat.

With plenty blaming manager Thomas Tuchel for negative tactics, “All players were afforded an opportunity to air their personal views during the meeting”, with “some of the squad” holding “grievances” after the game.

England were in a strong position to make their first World Cup final in 60 years when they came up against an Argentina side in Atlanta that had been dragged to the final four by Lionel Messi.

Despite the struggles of the reigning champions, however, the Albiceleste managed to get the job done late in the semi, overturning Anthony Gordon's opening strike to set up a showpiece against Spain in New Jersey – which they in turn lost.

According to the BBC's Sami Mokbel, a September meeting allowed for the squad to express how they felt about the collapse, which was blamed on Tuchel sitting back to protect the slender advantage against the brilliance of Messi.

As noted, “a number of senior England players held misgivings at Tuchel's instructions for the closing stages of the Argentina loss, believing the approach was too negative and defensive,” with “captain Harry Kane… strong and forthright with his views.”

Bellingham was mentioned by name, too, as being “particularly candid” in expressing that he felt his side were superior man-for-man to the opposition.

Real Madrid midfielder Bellingham re-established himself as one of his country's most important players in North America over the summer, despite heading into the tournament with question marks over how much of a role he would play under Tuchel.

The 23-year-old was in and out of the German's plans during qualification, with Morgan Rogers preferred at times in the No.10 role.

Bellingham has played 60 times for his country and scored 14 times. England host Croatia this Thursday night.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League group stage match between RB Leipzig and Manchester City from Saxony. The hosts started the day in 27th place in the 36-team table after two defeats, both by four goals to one, in away games against Como and Real Madrid. City begin proceedings in 12th after victories over Porto and AEK sandwiching that rip-roaring 4-2 defeat by the champions PSG at the Etihad.

City, who seemed in rude health after seven successive wins at the start of the Premier League campaign despite the guilty verdicts in the Premier League’s case against them for financial cheating, have wobbled since then, losing their last two league games. Marc Guéhi and Gigi Donnarumma are both suffering bouts of poor form, other individual errors continue to plague them and, although they are creating hatfuls of chances, they have been thwarted by a combination of imprecise finishing and the excellence of Zion Suzuki and Bart Verbruggen.

For all their travails on the road – RB Leipzig have also lost at Werder Bremen, Bayer Leverkusen and Bayern Munich – they have won all their home Bundesliga matches as well as a 1-0 victory over PSV in this competition. Their total of 22 league goals is second only to Bayern’s 27 and Antonio Nusa, a Norway team-mate of Erling Haaland, is in sparkling form flitting behind strikers Christopher Nkunku and Romulo. City, whose full-backs, if you can describe the centre-backs and midfielders who play either side of the centre-halves in that way, never look fit for purpose defensively and may well have their work cut out tonight if he drifts wide.

The Red Bull coaching principles, which have treated us to the dross football of Jesse Marsch, Matthias Jaissle and Ralph Hasenhüttl, all about the long pass, the central channel, counter-pressing and second balls, have a new proponent in Martín Demichelis, the forner City and Argentina defender who won the title in 2014 at the Etihad. Three years ago he led River Plate to the title in Argentina, the highlight of a coaching career also spent running Bayern’s U21s, Monterey and Mallorca.

These two have met six times in the last five years, City winning four, most notably the 7-0 thrashing at the Etihad in 2023’s Round of 16, the year they went on to win the Treble. Leipzig’s only victory came at home five years ago in the sixth, redundant group game when City and PSG had already clinched qualification for the knockout stages.

Antoine Semenyo is City’s only absentee; Leipzig will have to do without one-cap Germany midfielder Assan Ouédraogo and former Chelsea striker Marc Guiu.

The Manchester United hierarchy must not disregard relegation as an impossibility after one win in their opening 10 league matches this season

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada and technical director Jason Wilcox are scheduled to sit down with Sir Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco this week.

Head coach Michael Carrick’s future is expected to dominate the agenda at the pre-planned meeting in the principality where Ratcliffe is based. There is every chance a far more unpalatable subject will also be confronted given Man United's start to the 2026/27 season: drafting a contingency plan for relegation.

Ten games into the Premier League campaign, Man United find themselves in the bottom three with just a solitary victory. Minority owners INEOS arrived at Old Trafford boasting elite operating standards and a clear structure but on the pitch, the team has been dragged into a survival scrap for the second year running.

Acknowledging the drop remains something of a taboo for a club of Man United's size and commercial footprint, but a recent warning from north London shows why ignoring it would constitute negligence.

Speaking on The Sports Agents podcast, Tottenham Hotspur chief executive Vinai Venkatesham revealed how the club were planning for the future after Spurs flirted with disaster last season.

“It's really tough, because you form a relationship with people. Obviously, Igor [Tudor] wasn't the coach for long, but Thomas [Frank], we worked together really, really, really closely, went through some really difficult times," Venkatesham explained.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Spurs ultimately secured survival on the final day, but Venkatesham admitted the club had quietly mapped out a blueprint for the Championship.

“It was really challenging. A really, really, really challenging period for the club,” he said. “You have to [prepare for relegation]. I mean, you can't not. To not make that plan would have been irresponsible… Sometimes going through something as traumatic as what we went through last season bonds people a little bit and also puts even more fire in everybody's belly to make sure that something like that can never happen again.”

That brush with the drop motivated Spurs to spend £300 million on summer transfer targets, including £100m on Newcastle United's Sandro Tonali and £85m on West Ham United midfielder Matheus Fernandes.

“Everybody was aligned we wanted to strengthen this position, and then everybody was aligned that Matheus [Fernandes] was absolutely the number one target,” Venkatesham said. “If I'm honest, we achieved more than we thought we might do, and that was really because so many of our number one targets we were able to land. Because if we weren't going to get our number one targets, we weren't going to settle.”

Even with morale lifted by recent wins, Venkatesham reflected honestly on their sluggish start: “I wasn't worried [by the start to the 2026/27 season], but I was definitely frustrated… Did we think we were going to make this many changes and everything would gel straight away? Of course we didn't. But did we think we'd be hovering around the position of the league that we were in the international break? Of course we didn't either.”

For Ratcliffe, Berrada, and Wilcox, Venkatesham’s transparency should rid them of any lingering delusions of grandeur. Precedent proves that stature, revenue, and history offer little insulation once a club slips into the bottom three.

Whether Man United decide to back Carrick through the November break or sack him, the decision-making trio at the Monaco summit cannot afford to treat the drop as an unthinkable scenario.

That might mean re-thinking squad wage-reduction clauses or auditing broadcast revenue drop-offs, because after all, responsible governance demands preparing for the worst.

If Man United pretend they are simply too big to go down, that is the quickest way to end up there.

#1079. Biotech innovations are an opportunity to limit climate change

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Climate change is affecting many types of crop, including these unusually small potatoes.Credit: John Thys/AFP/Getty

Policymakers at the United Nations COP31 climate conference that started this week in Antalya, Turkey, will know that the UN Environment Programme has confirmed that global warming will exceed the limit of 1.5 °C above pre-industrial temperatures agreed in 2015 in Paris. This meeting comes hot on the heels of the UN COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, which affirmed yet again that the world is also in the middle of a biodiversity crisis. Progress in each case, whether preventing dangerous climate change or stemming biodiversity loss, is too slow. But researchers across scientific disciplines are now arguing that advances in biotechnology could provide solutions1. Methods such as gene editing and germplasm mining — the analysis of huge libraries of plant-genome sequences to find useful traits for crop improvement — can now be used to tackle global warming and protect nature, scientists write in a climate-themed issue of Nature Biotechnology.

There was a time — not that long ago — when many considered biotechnologies a threat to the environment. But as the special issue shows, a shift is under way. Now, the field offers strategies for protecting both climate and biodiversity from the many damaging effects of industrial agriculture.

To feed a growing global population, between 2015 and 2024, the amount of cultivated land grew by roughly eight million hectares a year1. Yet, if the greenhouse-gas emissions, and thus global warming, this expansion causes is to be avoided, the world must work out how to produce enough food within its current agricultural footprint. Land clearance and land-use change contributes up to five billion tonnes of carbon annually — and is a major cause of biodiversity loss. Here, biotech solutions have some of the greatest potential, for example, by helping to increase crop yields and to protect plants from heat, drought and disease.

How biotechnology can mitigate climate change by curbing the global land squeeze

How biotechnology can mitigate climate change by curbing the global land squeeze

Of 77 such technologies with applications in agriculture, aquaculture and other sectors, many are ready for large-scale testing in the field, propose bioengineers Shekhar Mishra, Lauren Lui and Adam Arkin at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California in a Perspective article2. Argentina, China and the United States have given the green light to engineered drought-tolerant crops.

Rice farming produces around 9% of human-caused emissions of the greenhouse gas methane. Now, researchers have found a way to slash these emissions, write agronomist Yunkai Jin at Hunan Agricultural University in Changsha, China, and his colleagues in a Comment article3.

But technological readiness isn’t enough: governments, regulators and the public need to be ready, too4. Readers might have a sense of déjà vu: in the 1990s, advances in biotechnology promised a revolution in food and agriculture — which subsequently stalled. The ambition was to genetically modify crops or engineer them in other ways so that they could tolerate herbicides, resist insects and fight viruses. But, at the time, many scientists, governments and corporations promoting the technology gave insufficient attention to several issues.

Deployability of biotechnologies for environmentally resilient agriculture

Deployability of biotechnologies for environmentally resilient agriculture

One concern was public anxiety about the idea of eating food produced using transgenic technologies — crops modified by inserting a gene from another plant species or other organism. Another issue was that risks to the environment and to human health had not been studied sufficiently. A third problem was that multinational companies dominated both the research and the development of these technologies, creating fears that the rise of agricultural biotechnology would put many small family farms out of business.

Environmental groups found common cause with consumer organizations. Together, they urged governments to enact strict regulations. In the European Union, for example, risks to human health and the environment needed to be assessed before technologies producing genetically modified organisms could be commercialized. Although this was necessary, it slowed down advances in low- and middle-income countries, because any nation intending to export produce to the EU would have to prove that it was not genetically modified.

Since then, at least two things have changed, increasing optimism about the use of biotechnology to help the planet. The discovery of gene editing — in which an organism’s genes are modified precisely to produce specific traits — has proved transformational for agriculture. The method is being developed cautiously and is regulated in a more nuanced way than were conventional technologies that produce genetically modified crops. In June, the EU amended its regulations on genetic modification and now permits the cultivation of some gene-edited crops.

Low-methane rice is near — the world should deploy it

Low-methane rice is near — the world should deploy it

A second development is that catastrophic events such as heatwaves and floods have meant that climate change and the planet’s protection have become mainstream concerns across science and society, not just for environmental research. In a way, we all need to be environmentalists now, and this provides a rationale for governments to reconsider adopting biotech solutions with appropriate safeguards in place.

Advances in biotechnology that limit land use should be deployed to slow down the rise in global temperatures and biodiversity loss. This will require a partnership between the private sector, scientists, conservationists and farmers. High-yielding crops produced using industrial agriculture have helped to feed the world but have also had a devastating effect on biodiversity. Organic agriculture is more sustainable but requires extra land, because its yields tend to be lower than those from industrial methods. Providing they are implemented wisely, safely and ethically, biotechnologies could contribute to innovative farming methods that offer the best of both worlds.

#1078. Tuchel: Bellingham and I were up and down – now we are in a good place

England head coach Thomas Tuchel described his relationship with Jude Bellingham as being “in a good place” after admitting it had been “a bit up and down”.

Tuchel has two Bellinghams in his latest England squad after calling up Jude’s brother, Jobe, for the first time for the Nations League games against Croatia and Spain. If they play together, it will be the first time brothers have represented England in the same team since Gary and Phil Neville 19 years ago.

This time last year, Tuchel cast doubt over Jude’s place in his team by picking Morgan Rogers over him, having not included the Real Madrid midfielder in an England squad the previous month.

But Jude performed superbly for Tuchel at the World Cup and was England’s best player during the last international camp. Tuchel revealed he has listened to his advice by calling up 21-year-old Jobe.

Asked if his relationship with Jude has developed, Tuchel said: “It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] of course, but we are in a good place.

“I love to be his coach, he’s a top player, a very influential player and it goes both ways. If Jude was not feeling comfortable, he would not perform at that level.

“At the moment, you see he’s happy to come into camp, he’s happy with the role he has, he’s fully invested and now to have the chance to have both of them [Bellingham brothers] is just the next step. I hope we have finished with the down. You never know as a coach.”

Jobe has captained England’s Under-21s and, as well as U21 head coach Lee Carlsey, Tuchel acknowledged the influence of Jude on the Borussia Dortmund midfielder’s first senior call.

Jude once said that playing with Jobe for England would be “the biggest dream of my life” and that it would mean more to him than any trophies.

Discussing Jude’s influence on Jobe’s selection, Tuchel said: “We spoke about his brother because I was aware it was always his dream and Jude was always like, ‘Watch him, he’s good, he can make it,’ I would say, ‘Yeah we are watching him.’ And we know, of course, from Lee Carsley and we see him with the Under-21s and there is such positive feedback.

“This is also the signal that if you are good in the Under-21s, this is the next step. We had it with Elliot Anderson, we had it with Alex Scott, we have it with Jarell Quansah and it counts. If you play good for England in the Under-19s, 20s, 21s, if you play good for England in tournaments then it means something.”

Tuchel at one point had to correct himself, with a laugh, when he accidentally referred to Jobe as Jube. On the subject of how Jobe reacted to his call-up and the comparisons with his brother that he will inevitably face, Tuchel said: “He has to live with this that everyone will compare them. They look similar, even in their movements, but they are very different players. And let’s see – they are also different characters, at least that’s what I heard.

“He [Jobe] watched training very early in my [reign]. In my first March camp maybe, he came over and watched his brother train. We chatted and we said, ‘Ah, it would be nice if one day you are with him [Jude].’ He was very kind and polite and I’m glad to have him in camp.

“He couldn’t stop smiling [when I told him]. He has the same beautiful smile as Jude, so it’s nice to have him. Let’s see what the effect is. What I saw, Jude was always the big brother that you imagine, taking care of his younger brother and making sure everything is alright. Behaving like a big brother. And that helps Jobe now. And it will be beautiful for Jude to have his brother close and in camp and to have this experience together. It’s a very special moment for them.”

The room is furnished in a typical Austrian style. Lots of wood, a fireplace, a few decorative touches. Through the large windows, you can see mountains surrounding the town of Saalfelden. Right on the dot, 21-year-old Jobe Bellingham arrives. It is August 2025, the midfielder has just signed for Borussia Dortmund and is giving his first press conference at the club’s training camp. German journalists are eager to find out what kind of character this talented youngster is. Will he provide any useful quotes for a story?

Half an hour later, the reporters are full of admiration and their notepads are full. Open-minded, self-assured, with clear opinions and a firm stance. That is how Bellingham presents himself. “It’s just not in my nature to be a superstar. I want to function like a machine,” he says. That was 15 months ago – a lot has happened since.

The Dortmund hierarchy knew Bellingham would need time to adapt to the Bundesliga. Internally, the message had always been that the first season would be a settling-in period, despite the hefty transfer fee of around €30 million (£25m). His first year was a mixed bag. However, there was one thing that impressed the club’s leadership every day: the way Bellingham constantly pushed himself to improve. His level of motivation is unmatched in the squad. His fitness numbers back that up. Kovac, a firm believer in discipline and physical conditioning, has the squad’s physical performance metrics reviewed on a regular basis. For him, they are the foundation of success. And in virtually every analysis, Bellingham ranks among the very best. The extra work he puts in beyond official training sessions is paying off.

Kovac says: “Jobe came from the English second tier; that’s a completely different game. It’s much slower there. The intensity in the Bundesliga is the highest of any of Europe’s top leagues. We run more, we sprint more. Jobe has developed physically. We always knew he could play football. But one thing leads to another. He’s settled in Germany.”

For his club, Bellingham is far more than just a midfielder. He is also a figurehead and a driving force behind the club’s marketing activities. The Bellingham name, made famous by his brother Jude, who played for Dortmund from 2020 to 2023 before moving to Real Madrid for almost €130m (£108m), is arguably the most recognisable in Dortmund’s squad. When the club embarked on a marketing tour of Asia last summer, Bellingham was front and centre. At a Puma event in Osaka, he addressed the guests. In Tokyo, where the Dortmund delegation travelled next, a film about BVB was projected on to a huge skyscraper. The central figure: Jobe Bellingham. And after the public training sessions, Japanese supporters were particularly eager to get photos with him.

Jobe never wanted to be a carbon copy of his brother. He wanted to write his own story. The club, too, has resisted direct comparisons. They just wanted Jobe, not the younger brother of a world-class star. Now the brothers will be reunited in the England squad. For Jude, it is a dream come true. He previously said: “We’ve played together on the streets for so long. Playing for England alongside my brother would be the greatest dream of my life. That would mean more to me than any trophy.”

Dortmund have never fought harder for a player in recent years than Bellingham. The club’s executives first met him in person in the summer of 2020, when Jude signed. Jobe accompanied his brother to Germany. From that moment on, the club monitored every step of his development: his progress through the youth ranks at Birmingham City, the family club of the Bellinghams, and the evolution of his positioning on the pitch. After all, as a child, Jobe was still playing as a centre-forward. Over time, however, he gradually moved into deeper roles.

In May 2025, BVB decided to make their move. Word had reached Dortmund that Eintracht Frankfurt were interested and had already invited Bellingham to their training facilities. The pressure was on. Dortmund responded by pulling out all the stops. President Hans-Joachim Watzke, the man who shaped the club for more than two decades and led it to the top of German football, stepped in. He flew to England and met Bellingham face to face. It was a secret mission. Watzke was determined not to attract any attention that could jeopardise negotiations.

The problem: Sunderland, Bellingham’s former club, had secured promotion to the Premier League only a day earlier. Hundreds of supporters were gathered outside the hotel where Watzke and Bellingham were due to meet. To avoid being recognised, Watzke put on sunglasses and a cap before making his way through the crowd. He brought two gifts with him. Firstly, a BVB shirt with Jobe’s name on the back. Secondly, a handwritten note from Kovac expressing his desire to work with the midfielder. A few days later, Watzke received a phone call. It was Jobe. His decision had been made. He was joining Dortmund.

Ever since, the midfielder has enjoyed almost unwavering support. Watzke frequently spoke with him throughout his first season, offering encouragement and reassurance. The same was true of Kovac and other senior figures. Equally important to his breakthrough has been team-mate Felix Nmecha, with whom Bellingham has developed a close friendship and who has become an important source of advice. When time allows, the two enjoy playing padel together. Off the pitch they are opponents; on it they form a midfield partnership.

And while his father Mark was still complaining to club officials around a year ago that his son was not getting enough playing time, the situation has changed dramatically. The Bellingham family are delighted, and his England call-up has provided further confirmation that he is on the right path.

Thomas Tuchel has Jordan Henderson back fit – and playing well – since the last international break. The last of Henderson’s 91 caps came at the World Cup against Panama, with his tournament effectively ended when he famously broke his arm in the celebrations at the Azteca after Mexico were defeated. From Tuchel’s squad in the summer, Djed Spence has also returned from injury although he is only just back playing for Inter Milan.

Marcus Rashford is set to miss out on England through injury having barely played since the last international break. The Manchester United forward pulled out of the last squad, then returned for his club the following weekend. But he has not featured since the defeat to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League. His absence will open up a space for another wide forward, with Noni Madueke pushing for a call-up with his form for Arsenal.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the announcement by Thomas Tuchel of England’s squad for their remaining two Uefa Nations Group 3 matches against Croatia – them again – at Wembley next Thursday and Spain at the Metropolitano in Madrid next Sunday night. England have already qualified for the knockout phase – barring a defeat by Croatia by a margin of eight or more goals – but would need two victories to avoid France and Portugal in the next two-legged phase in March.

Tuchel’s only major injury doubt from the last squad are Arsenal’s Bukao Saka and Como’s Trevoh Chalobah as well as the more long-term absentee Tino Livramento, the man Chalobah replaced in the World Cup 26. Djed Spence has returned to full fitness and played for Inter in their Milan derby defeat last weekend while the head coach’s favourite player, Jordan Henderson, has been passed fit to play for Chelsea at his boyhood club Sunderland on Sunday though at 36 his race may finally have been run at this level despite his unexpected encore in the last 18 months.

For the first time since 2001 England will have the Ballon d’Or winner in the squad and Harry Kane will also become England’s most-capped player – barring some misfortune when Bayern Munich take on Mainz on Saturday – by leading them out at Wembley on Thursday night for his 126th appearance.

Whether he will be joined by Cole Palmer in the squad remains the only significant issue of note. The Chelsea forward pulled out of the last squad as part of his club’s management of his groin injury but he has played in their last four Premier League games, scoring once and being sent off once as well. Kobbie Mainoo is fit again and may be picked to see if his backside has recovered from bench splinters since his summer of exasperation.

The squad will be released at 10am and followed by Tuchel’s explanations, which we will also cover here, an hour later.

Arsenal are set to lose a major first-teamer in the January transfer market

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Arsenal are on the cusp of losing a major star this January.

The Gunners enjoyed a solid if not spectacular summer transfer window, bringing in Bruno Guimaraes, Ezri Konsa and Christos Tzolis to add quality and depth to a title-winning side.

But with competition fierce for places, it appears that one Arsenal player is set to leave to seek game time elsewhere.

Mikel Arteta's side are top of the Premier League table, five points clear, unbeaten in the Champions League, and have only lost twice in all competitions this season.

But not everyone is happy with their role in N5, and now, RNE Deportes originally broke the news of a departure, with further updated relayed in a report by Sport Witness.

Martin Zubimendi is on the cusp of leaving for Atletico Madrid, as per Relevo, with his relationship with Arteta said to be “cold”, following “friction towards the end of last season”.

Another Spanish outlet, AS, adds that Arsenal need to sell, and would like to recoup the £50 million they spent on the Basque midfielder.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Zubimendi only moved to the Emirates Stadium in 2025, with the Gunners beating a host of rivals for his signature after a star turn in the Euro 2024 final.

The 27-year-old became an instant hit alongside Declan Rice in Arteta's engine room, providing the progression and anticipation that the side had missed in that area of the pitch, becoming almost ever-present in the first half of Arsenal's title-winning season.

But as the season neared the run-in, Zubimendi found himself dropped in favour of Hale Ender, Myles Lewis-Skelly, and didn't start the Champions League final – with Arsenal upgrading in the summer to sign Bruno Guimaraes.

Zubimendi has not started a single league game in midfield for Arsenal this term, finding himself fourth in the pecking order in midfield.

FourFourTwo understands that Arsenal would rather not sell the World Cup winner this January and would prefer to wait until the summer to assess the situation further.

Zubimendi is worth €65m, according to Transfermarkt. Arsenal travel away to Newcastle United when Premier League action resumes after the international break.

Jack Grealish's Everton travails could signal a death knell to the 'Gazza generation'

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Deep down, Jack Grealish will know that his fate extends beyond Everton's season.

English football’s first £100m player has won multiple Premier League titles and a Champions League yet still faces a fight to stave off the death knell to an increasingly lost generation as much as his own elite-level career.

Grealish again finds himself out in the cold after a ‘breach of club discipline’ in the run-up to Everton’s Carabao Cup win over Newcastle and was subsequently deemed unfit for the league rematch at St James’ Park on Monday night. On both occasions, David Moyes’s side were hardly poorer without the winger’s presence.

The Toffees are yet to decide on a definitive course of action over Grealish’s reported unauthorised absence from training, but patience is now in increasingly short supply from the club and its supporters alike. At a time when Moyes is dealing with crippling squad dearth - just 18 senior players were left after a disastrous summer window - the England international's latest misdemeanour threw him another needless curveball.

There was always a risk that Grealish's propensity to hit the headlines for the wrong reasons would again rear its head on Merseyside, where he claimed that feeling ‘loved’ in his initial loan spell was a driving factor in embarking on a second. Such was a fondness for his current surroundings that he undertook the bulk of his rehabilitation from a season-ending foot injury sustained in January at their Finch Farm training ground instead of returning to parent club Manchester City.

But even then, indiscretion was still lurking round the corner. When Everton slipped to a late April defeat at relegation candidates West Ham, Grealish was being snapped slumped against the arm of a chair in a Manchester rooftop bar surrounded by bottles and glasses. Now 31, he is in danger of completing an unholy trinity that was once touted for greatness as successors to Paul Gascoigne’s throne but allowed their careers to crash and burn.

Just 16 months separate the respective birth dates of the Birmingham-born talent, Dele Alli and Raheem Sterling. All three were alive when English football’s flawed genius enjoyed one last hurrah at Euro 96 but none will have any memories of it. That has still done little to stop their affection for ‘Gazzamania’ running deep.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Upon his return to Everton this summer, Grealish revealed he was partly inspired to take the No.18 shirt worn by Gascoigne during a forgettable and fleeting spell in the blue half of Merseyside while Sterling also cited the man that personified the 1990 World Cup as his all-time favourite Three Lions player. Even Dele, who himself previously sought redemption at Everton, made an embarrassing attempt at recreating the infamous ‘dentist’s chair’ celebration during a training session at Euro 2016.

They also appeared destined to follow in his footsteps by earning moves to high-profile leagues overseas with Real Madrid heavily touted as a future destination for each player. Beyond personal homages, Gascoigne has become intertwined with the trio as a quickfire buzzword for their respective rises to prominence. Individual billings as the ‘new Gazza’ also proved to be a self-fulfilling prophecy for a penchant for self-destruction mirroring the downfall of the former Rangers and Lazio playmaker. Dele is now 14 months into unofficial retirement and resorting to calling up former teammates live on Twitch streams in a desperate ploy to stay in the public consciousness. An awkward attempted catch-up with Harry Kane, just weeks before his old Tottenham sparring partner claimed the Ballon d’Or, lasted barely 60 seconds.

The depth of Dele's continental ambitions was short-lived spells with Besiktas and Como, making a solitary appearance for the latter before being released barely midway through an 18-month contract. Free agent Sterling fared far worse with a three-month spell at Feyenoord which was terminated last season. Grealish's former City teammate and fellow Euro 2020 standout faces the real prospect of ending this month behind bars as well as without a club after pleading guilty to dangerous driving while inhaling nitrous oxide and crashing his Lamborghini on the A327 in May.

Without sufficient intervention on his own part, Grealish may soon follow his former contemporaries in falling by the footballing wayside. More than most, he has been the poster boy for Gascoigne's heirs, as the man himself confirmed to FourFourTwo last year by singling out the former Aston Villa graduate as his closest embodiment in the current crop of players. His exploits in City’s 2023 treble-winning campaign hinted that England’s first Ballon d’Or winner since Michael Owen was closer than Kane’s recent triumph but never came to pass. What happens next will be era-defining.

Grealish is still capable of technical excellency, as demonstrated in a truncated first loan spell with Everton, if he can stave off personal indiscipline issues. He would not be the first homegrown talent to do so. Ross Barkley, another ex-teammate born in the mid-90s, was also festooned with the Gascoigne moniker yet managed to overcome his own off-field issues to earn a second chance at Villa. Persistent injuries prevented the playmaker from scaling even a fraction of the heights he was originally tipped to reach but used stints at Nice and Luton Town to rebuild his reputation and earn a bit-part role with Unai Emery’s side.

By personal admission, Grealish has been his own worst enemy when it comes to a sense of timing off the pitch which is at odds with an often impeccable nature on it. Unless he can conquer those social demons which ultimately brought down his idol as well as those in the same talent pool, the epitaph of the 'Gazza generation' will be one of frustratingly unfulfilled potential.
