Former Southampton and Manchester United midfielder Morgan Schneiderlin explains why he thinks Mauricio Pochettino will be a success at Old Trafford

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United look set to change manager following a run of just one win in 10 league matches under Michael Carrick.

Mauricio Pochettino is in the picture to replace Carrick, meanwhile former Old Trafford and Southampton midfielder Morgan Schneiderlin has delivered an emphatic endorsement of the Argentine coach.

Pochettino is widely considered the leading candidate to take charge, and Schneiderlin - who played the finest football of his career under the Argentine at St Mary’s Stadium - insists the 54-year-old has the personal qualities required to unify a fractured club.

Reflecting on Pochettino’s arrival in English football in 2013, Schneiderlin revealed that an initial language barrier did nothing to dilute the manager’s authority.

"He didn't need to speak a lot of the language," Schneiderlin recalls, via Comeon.com. "He would put an arm around you, and with the translator or someone who spoke English, he’d explain what he liked about you and exactly what he wanted you to do.

"I'll always remember his team talk before that first game against Everton. He was just screaming in Spanish, a deeply motivational speech, entirely in Spanish, but all we could hear and understand was: 'Press like lions! Press like lions! Press like lions!' And we did press like lions!

"Now that he speaks fluent English, it's going to be even easier for him. But his charisma, his presence, and the way he carried himself - we were just under his spell straight away."

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That buy-in was cemented on the Saints' training ground, where Pochettino instituted a relentless physical culture.

"We were working very, very hard in training sessions and in the gym, not to be bodybuilders or look nice on the beach, but building a lot of lower-body strength," Schneiderlin explains.

"He used me much more as a true box-to-box midfielder - he wanted me to run, to press, and to win the ball back. It was very enjoyable."

However, Schneiderlin has warned against expecting Pochettino to instantly rely on academy graduates to dig Man United out of trouble, stressing that Old Trafford 'demands results immediately' and requires a stable footing first.

Having since managed Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea, Pochettino will set foot inside Old Trafford a more battle-hardened version of the coach who took charge at Southampton 13 years ago.

"He arrives now with so much experience behind him and so much baggage, both good and bad, he has learned from," Schneiderlin added. "He will use everything he learned from being in Paris Saint-Germain dealing with big players and big personalities."

#1048. Michael Carrick sacked by Man United with club stuck in relegation zone after latest crisis

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

United have failed to win in eight Premier League games and will spend the international break 18th in the table

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Michael Carrick has been sacked as Manchester United manager with the club sitting in the Premier League relegation places after 10 games.

A second Old Trafford comeback of the week, this time battling from two goals down twice to rescue a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday, could not save Carrick’s job and he departs United just three months into the start of the season and with his side 18th during the international break.

United ended a nine-game winless run when they came from two goals down to beat Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday but they have not won in eight attempts in the Premier League and have just one top-flight win this campaign.

It represents a stark turnaround from Carrick’s positive impact as interim manager last season, when the former midfielder went beyond expectations after replacing Ruben Amorim in January, steadying the ship and guiding them to Champions League qualification.

Carrick’s position has been under threat since the damaging defeats against Como and Bournemouth last month, but he survived crisis talks with the United hierarchy and was given time to turn results around, but speculation over a change begun the day after Sunday’s chaotic draw and United States boss Mauricio Pochettino is expected to succeed Carrick having reportedly reached a verbal agreement with the club.

United have made contact with US Soccer over compensation for Pochettino with a reported figure of $10m (£7.4m) set to be paid to release him from his contract which was due to run through to the 2030 World Cup. His current staff are set to join him at Old Trafford and would require further compensation payments.

The timing of the November international break, with a full two weeks before their next game away to Liverpool in the Premier League, has prompted United to finally act and leave minority owners Ineos searching for a fourth permanent manager in three years.

Though Pochettino is the overwhelming favourite to become the next head coach, Eddie Howe is available following his departure from Newcastle in the summer while former Bayern Munich and Germany manager Julian Nagelsmann is also an option. Aston Villa’s Unai Emery and Brighton’s Fabian Hurzeler are admired but their clubs would demand significant compensation.

Manchester United confirmed the news of Carrick’s exit with a statement which reads: “Manchester United can confirm that Michael Carrick has departed his role as men’s first-team head coach.

“Michael rejoined the club in January and guided the team to a third-placed Premier League finish by winning 12 out of the remaining 17 games of the 2025/26 season, accumulating the highest points tally in the league during that period.

“After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions.

“Michael is, and always will be, a Manchester United legend. Just as he did as a player, he has conducted himself with the highest standards of dedication and professionalism throughout his time back with the club. His leadership and achievements last season will always be fondly remembered.

“The club intends to appoint a permanent successor as quickly as possible.”

Carrick initially returned to Old Trafford as interim manager – his second stint in caretaker role – after the dismissal of Amorim at the beginning of the year. He was rewarded with the full-time position after guiding United to third in the Premier League last term and securing a return to the Champions League.

United spent £155m on three new midfielders this summer – signing Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans and Andre Santos, after missing out on their top targets Elliott Anderson and Sandro Tonali – but failed to sign a back-up left-back to Luke Shaw or another forward to support the injury-prone Benjamin Sesko.

But defender Lisandro Martinez criticised the club’s hierarchy for not doing more to support Carrick following the 2-1 defeat to Atletico Madrid earlier this month while captain Bruno Fernandes questioned his manager’s tactics following the 4-1 loss at Como a week later.

Carrick had gambled by dropping captain Fernandes for the home match against Bournemouth but a dismal 3-0 defeat instead highlighted how a fractured dressing room has unravelled since the beginning of the season.

Carrick said Fernandes did not play against Bournemouth due to “pure football” reasons before holding clear-the-air talks with the Portuguese and selecting him to start as his captain in the game at Stamford Bridge.

Another defeat followed against Chelsea before United finally ended their losing run by beating Roma. The stirring win did not save Carrick’s job, however, even after another remarkable comeback against Aston Villa on Sunday.

United have conceded 30 goals in their 14 games this season and have won just three times – against newly promoted Ipswich in the Premier League and Sabah and Roma in Europe. They will travel to Liverpool on 22 November having spent the fortnight in the bottom three.

Mauricio Pochettino took over at Southampton back in 2013 and has gone on to manage some of the world's biggest clubs since

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mauricio Pochettino’s managerial career in English football first materialised because Southampton officials travelled to Spain to scout Philippe Coutinho, the Argentine revealed in an exclusive interview with FourFourTwo earlier this year.

With Pochettino now heavily linked with and expected to take over the Manchester United post, more light is being shed on the 52-year-old's initial move to the Premier League.

In January 2013, Southampton dismissed Nigel Adkins despite the club sitting in relative safety following back-to-back promotions. Chairman Nicola Cortese appointed Pochettino, who had left Espanyol two months earlier. The connection, however, was made while Cortese and sporting director Paul Mitchell were running checks on Coutinho, who was on loan at the Catalan side from Inter Milan, and would later complete an £8.5 million transfer to Liverpool.

"In England, nobody knew who I was," Pochettino said. "[Former Southampton chairman] Nicola Cortese is another key figure in my career. They were tracking Philippe Coutinho, who was on loan with us at Espanyol, and came to a match.

"Both Nicola and the sporting director, Paul Mitchell, became interested in the way I coached and expressed myself on the touchline. Six months later, they called me to take the job. Nicola took a real gamble – he had the courage to make that appointment because the club was in a comfortable position in the Premier League, having achieved back-to-back promotions. It was a risky move for him, but he also knew what we were capable of doing."

Pochettino's arrival at St Mary’s was initially met with scepticism in the English press due to the timing of Adkins’ sacking, particularly given he initially conducted post-match interviews in Spanish with the help of a translator. However, the Argentine explained that a language barrier helped shield him from the immediate fallout.

"Not at all," Pochettino said when asked if the reaction generated any undue pressure. "We were young and full of confidence. I had the advantage of not speaking English at the beginning, so I wasn’t reading or listening to anything – I paid no attention to the media.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"I was a bit isolated from everything, living in my own bubble. My assistant Jesus Perez acted as a filter and only told me what was truly important."

Pochettino quickly implemented an aggressive, high-pressing system on the south coast, leaning heavily on young domestic talent including current Man United defender Luke Shaw and future Liverpool midfielder Adam Lallana.

"We had players who were physically like jets, perfectly suited to how we wanted to play – a style built on aggression and intensity," Pochettino said.

"Technically they were good, but the best thing was their potential to improve even further. We were a perfect match.

"In England, the ones who began to introduce a different kind of football were Brendan Rodgers at Liverpool and us at Southampton, with our build-up and high attacking press."

With Man United's hierarchy holding talks over Michael Carrick's position following a return of one win from ten league games, Pochettino is very much in the frame to be the next man up. For a manager now positioned to take over at Old Trafford, his initial entry into English football remains tied to a scouting trip for an ex-Liverpool star.

#1046. Football fan arrest numbers branded ‘unacceptable’ by policing chief

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Police praised supporters who travelled to North America for their conduct but warned that wider football-related disorder remains a concern

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Latest arrest figures for fans watching last summer’s World Cup are "unacceptably" high despite excluding linked crimes such as domestic abuse, football’s policing lead has said.

Home Office data shows 357 arrests occurred in England and Wales linked to fans watching England matches during the North American tournament, compared to just 19 arrests at the event itself.

Chief Constable Mark Hobrough, National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC) lead for football policing, praised travelling fans for "exemplary" behaviour, but described conduct at home during the World Cup and 2025-26 domestic season as far more troubling.

He said: "Though the vast majority of supporters attending domestic fixtures in the UK are law-abiding and enjoy supporting their teams at great games, there still remain an unacceptable number who spoil the event for others.

"2,025 people were arrested for football-related incidents during the domestic season in 2025-26, and disappointingly this number is up from 2,004 in 2024-25.

"In addition, 357 people were arrested in England and Wales for football-related incidents during the 2026 World Cup alone.

"Sadly, these figures do not paint a full picture as they do not include many of the associated offences, such as domestic abuse, which often occur behind closed doors after the full-time whistle has blown and in many cases nowhere near any stadium or club with individuals who’ve not attended any game themselves.

"However, as the figures show, we are continuing to take action against those responsible, and moving forward, we will continue to work with our partners including the Crown Prosecution Service, the Premier League, the EFL and the Football Association to collectively make football a safe environment for the overwhelming majority of supporters who just want to enjoy the game."

Home Office figures for 2025-26, first released in July showing 1,963 football-related arrests or police actions, have now been revised to 2,025.

Total arrests across the 2025-26 season—including domestic games, the World Cup, and European fixtures abroad—reached 2,403, falling from 2,584 in 2023-24, the previous men’s tournament season.

Tournament-related arrests within England and Wales increased compared to 2023-24, a change the Home Office attributed to better recording and awareness among police forces.

#1045. Man United Supporters’ Trust underlines ‘depressing moment’ after Michael Carrick sacked

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The supporters’ group said “responsibility for United’s problems... lie with the ownership” rather than Carrick

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The Manchester United Supporters’ Trust (MUST) has branded Michael Carrick’s sacking “another depressing moment” and argued the club’s problems rest primarily with its ownership, in a now-familiar plea to end the ongoing feeling of crisis at Old Trafford.

United sacked Carrick just 10 games into the Premier League season with the club in the relegation zone and having won just once in this domestic campaign.

The club’s hierarchy met minority owner Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco on Wednesday to discuss Carrick’s future and a statement on Thursday said that it had “come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions”.

Former Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea manager Mauricio Pochettino, who currently manages the US men’s national team, is in line to replace him.

The club statement paid tribute to former midfielder Carrick as a “Manchester United legend” and the MUST statement concurred, saying “his standing among supporters remains undiminished”, but criticised the ownership for the spiral the club has found itself in.

It said: “Michael Carrick’s departure marks another depressing moment for Manchester United. We thank him for his service and for restoring hope during the second half of last season. His standing among supporters remains undiminished.

“The reason Manchester United fans have continued to support Michael Carrick in recent weeks is that they know that responsibility for United’s problems do not primarily rest with him or indeed his predecessors as manager. They lie with the ownership.

“The Glazers’ debt-funded takeover continues to burden the club. When Ineos came in they promised sporting excellence, but yet with repeated changes in football leadership we have seen anything but.

“It is time for the owners to explain themselves and show some accountability.”

MUST continued to criticise “aggressive ticketing policies” which “have further damaged relations with supporters”, arguing “supporters are being asked to pay the price for the owners’ mismanagement as well as their stadium ambitions through higher charges and diminished rights”.

It continued: “The unprecedented scale of the booing at Old Trafford, alongside public criticism from senior players in recent weeks, now points to a deeper deterioration. These are signs of a club becoming more divided, with the bond between supporters, players and those running Manchester United under increasing strain.”

Defender Lisandro Martinez criticised the club’s hierarchy for not doing more to support Carrick in the transfer market following the 2-1 Champions League defeat to Atletico Madrid last month, while dire on-pitch performances have resulted in protests against the ownership and loud booing of the players, although there were public displays of support for Carrick by fans at Old Trafford.

MUST concluded: “The owners must allow senior club management to change direction: show accountability, rebuild trust, listen to supporters and recognise that their loyalty is fundamental to football success.

“Another change of head coach cannot repair what the ownership continues to undermine.”

The 2026 NWSL Championship is just two games away, with four teams remaining in the race for the title.

Reigning champions Gotham FC are still in contention after edging past Seattle Reign, while Washington Spirit, Kansas City Current and Utah Royals have also booked their places in the semi-finals.

With the final four now confirmed, two intriguing matchups await on November 14 and 15, as the teams battle for a place in the Championship match in Washington.

The 2026 NWSL playoffs began last weekend with the top eight teams battling it out for a place in the semi-finals, following a regular season in which Gotham FC emerged as the team to beat.

The defending champions finished top of the standings to claim the NWSL Shield for a first time and secure the No. 1 seed, while Washington Spirit, San Diego Wave, Kansas City Current, Angel City, Portland Thorns, Utah Royals and Seattle Reign also booked their places.

The first three quarter-finals were all decided by a single goal. Utah Royals pulled off the biggest upset, beating second seeds San Diego Wave 1-0 to secure their first-ever post-season victory.

Kansas City Current also edged through, with Michelle Cooper converting an extra-time penalty to seal a 1-0 win over Angel City.

Gotham also needed just one goal to overcome Seattle Reign, with an early own goal from Jordyn Bugg proving decisive.

Washington Spirit, meanwhile, delivered the standout performance of the round, sweeping aside Portland Thorns 4-1. Trinity Rodman scored twice, while Clara Luvanga contributed a goal and two assists.

The semi-final line-up is now confirmed, with Washington hosting Utah on November 14 before Gotham take on Kansas City the following day. The winners will meet in the Championship final at Audi Field on November 21.

Shaw has been one of Gotham's most influential attacking players this season, leading the team with 11 goals and five assists. The 21-year-old can create moments of brilliancem, through her movement, dribbling or eye for goal. Having returned from injury to start the quarter-final against Seattle, her availability and fitness could be particularly important as Gotham look to defend their title.

While Temwa Chawinga will often steal the headlines, Bethune has also enjoyed an outstanding season at Kansas City, setting a new NWSL single-season record with 11 assists. The midfielder's creativity and ability to unlock opposition defences will be crucial against a Gotham side that conceded just 23 goals during the regular season. With two-time MVP Chawinga providing a constant attacking threat beside her, KC Current's attacking line is one to be feared.

Rodman has been central to Washington's success this season, recording a career-best 12 goals and eight assists in the regular season. The forward carried that form into the quarter-finals, scoring twice and providing an assist in the 4-1 victory over Portland. Named an NWSL MVP finalist, she will be one of the biggest threats for Utah to contain.

Lacasse has been one of Utah's most productive players this season, contributing eight goals and 10 assists in the regular campaign. Her ability to create chances as well as find the net will be vital if the Royals are to continue their impressive play-off run. The 33-year-old played a key role in their quarter-final victory over second seeds San Diego Wave, providing the assist for Kiana Palacios' winning goal and Utah will be hoping she can help them produce another upset against Washington Spirit.

Prediction: Washington Spirit 3-1 Utah Royals

Utah have already shown they should not be underestimated, eliminating second seeds San Diego Wave away from home. Their defensive organisation and ability to take their chances make them a dangerous opponent.

However, Washington will be full of confidence after their emphatic quarter-final victory over Portland. With Trinity Rodman in outstanding form and the backing of a home crowd at Audi Field, they should have enough attacking quality to reach another Championship final...which is also to be played at Audi Field.

Prediction: Gotham FC 1-2 Kansas City Current

While defending champions Gotham finished the regular season with the league's best defensive record, conceding just 23 goals in 30 matches, Kansas City have the attacking firepower to trouble any side in the league.

Bethune's creativity and Chawinga's threat in front of goal will test Gotham's defence, while Kansas City's ability to score from different areas makes them particularly difficult to contain. Gotham's experience of winning on the biggest stage cannot be overlooked, but Kansas City have the quality to end the reigning champions' hopes of back-to-back titles.

#1043. McIlroy boosts Race to Dubai hopes as Luiten grabs shock lead

Joost Luiten holds a one-shot lead over Jacob Skov Olesen at the DP World Tour Championship; Rory McIlroy in tied third as he looks to overtake Eugenio Chacarra in the Race to Dubai standings; watch live on Friday from 7am on Sky Sports Golf

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Rory McIlroy made a strong start to his bid for a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title, as Joost Luiten grabbed a shock early lead at the DP World Tour Championship.

McIlroy, who needs to finish fourth or better to have a chance of surpassing Eugenio Chacarra in the season-long standings and win the Race to Dubai for an eighth time, carded an opening-round 69 at Jumeirah Golf Estates.

The world No 2 mixed five birdies with two bogeys in breezy conditions on the Earth Course, where he missed an eagle opportunity at the par-five last that would have moved him above Chacarra in the projected Race to Dubai standings.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

McIlroy sits in tied-third on three under and within two shots of Luiten, the last player in the field and 56th in the season rankings, who jumped top of the leaderboard after a five-under 67.

Jacob Skov Olesen briefly shared the lead but is one behind Luiten on four under, with Victor Perez, Gregorio De Leo, Freddy Schott and Francesco Laporta all two back alongside McIlroy, while Race to Dubai leader Chacarra opened with a level-par 72.

McIlroy can guarantee Race to Dubai victory by winning this event for a fourth time, with The Masters champion making the dream start by rolling in an eight-foot birdie at the first.

He responded to a three-putt par at the second by birdieing the par-three fourth, then bounced back from a sloppy three-putt from 15 feet at the fifth by taking advantage of the par-five seventh.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Chacarra was over-par until his three-birdie run from the seventh, seeing both reach the turn in 34, before McIlroy holed a birdie from the fringe to briefly get within two of the lead.

The leading pair in the Race to Dubai stumbled slightly over the closing stretch, with Chacarra making two bogeys in three holes from the 13th and McIlroy dropping a shot at the par-five 14th after missing the green with his third shot.

McIlroy hit a glorious approach to within 15 feet at the par-five last to leave a late eagle look, which would have seen him leapfrog Chacarra, although he had to settle for a two-putt birdie after leaving his effort short.

Luiten was in the first pair out on the opening morning and raced to the top of the leaderboard with a front-nine 31, then cancelled out back-to-back bogeys from the 11th by birdieing the 13th and 18th to reclaim top spot.

Olesen is also among those looking to secure PGA Tour membership - available to the top 10 eligible players in the Race to Dubai rankings, with the Dane's final-hole birdie getting him within one of Luiten, on a day where only 22 of the 50-man field finished under-par.

McIlroy was among nine players starting the week with a mathematical chance of topping the Race to Dubai rankings, but Jon Rahm and Daniel Hillier - who both carded one-under 71s - the only others to break par on the opening day.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Casey Jarvis, Jayden Schaper and Ryan Fox - who need a victory to have any chance of claiming No 1 - all started the week with a two-over 74, while major winner Aaron Rai struggled to an opening-round 76.

Rory McIlroy, following a three-under 69: "Anything in the 60s today I felt was a good score. And sort of held it together nicely when I needed to. It was nice to finish with a birdie at the last, and obviously in a pretty good position going into the next few days."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Race to Dubai leader Eugenio Chacarra: "I need to do a couple of things better to be able to have a chance on Sunday, and that's what I'm going to focus on. I think if I fix those, a little strategy-wise and I can putt a little better, I think I'm going to have a chance.

Joost Luiten, following his opening-round 67: "A good opening round. Had a great front nine, five under after nine, then you hope you can push on. The wind picked up and I made two annoying bogeys on 11 and 12. I'm quite happy finishing five under."

#1042. Destiny brought Mauricio Pochettino to Man United - but one huge question remains

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Argentine has come close to becoming Manchester United manager on three separate prior occasions. Now the stars appear to have finally aligned, but is it too late for either the man or the club?

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

On Sunday evening, Mauricio Pochettino got the call he had been waiting for.

He and long-time assistant Jesus Perez had frequently asked about Manchester United over the last decade. They would often contact friends in the game who were connected to Old Trafford, looking to find out what was happening, whether there could be an opening.

Pochettino came very close to taking one of those openings on at least three occasions: 2018, 2021 and 2024. Now, elements might finally have aligned.

It is a call that others at Old Trafford have long waited for, too. Back when they had a much publicised dinner in 2016, Sir Alex Ferguson essentially told Pochettino he should be the United manager. The Argentine was enthralled at that meeting by stories from one of the game’s great glory eras, and a sense of magic he had felt just standing in Old Trafford had been deepened.

Pochettino had been especially taken by Ferguson’s account of rebuilding United from the 1980s, initially drawing comparisons with what he was doing at Tottenham Hotspur. Now, he’s set to take on that exact same job, if one that has become so much bigger than in 2016. It is arguably even bigger than in 1986.

Pochettino, however, is fired by the idea of being the man to finally fix United. It has become one of the great managerial quests. The United hierarchy have ultimately gone for him because of that personality, and his standing. They don’t want a coach who hasn’t worked at this level. They want someone ready. Both the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe can sense that, since the two sides of the United ownership have known Pochettino for years.

If this is an appointment that always felt destined, though, that does raise one big question. Is this the right moment for it? Is it like Jose Mourinho, in that it came too late? Is it typical of modern United in that sense? Is it the same old “magical thinking” of hoping a famous name saves them, when the game has changed and the actual problems are now so structural?

Pochettino probably should have gone to United in 2016 or 2018, when he was at a peak in terms of being one of the most exciting coaches in football. The club did consider a move in the summer of 2016, but sources say an exit clause was allowed to expire. How different things could have been.

Old Trafford insiders are now talking about the value of “a name”, but the hierarchy did pass on Pochettino in 2024, when they initially considered sacking Erik ten Hag before ultimately deciding to stick with the Dutchman. His interview wasn’t seen as convincing as that of Thomas Tuchel or Roberto De Zerbi. Those who know him also say he is closer to being “a manager” now, in terms of a wider outlook, rather than the on-the-grass coach that so drove Spurs.

The very fact United are negotiating to pry him from the United States national team, without wishing to be disrespectful, also illustrates how his stock has recently dropped. Some close to Pochettino would nevertheless put that down to necessary choices at certain moments. Taking charge of the hosts of the biggest World Cup ever, that had so much pomp around it, was too enticing. Before that, he probably should have pushed to go to United or Real Madrid in 2018 but he was convinced he could do something special with Spurs. He’d put too much into it.

And that does point to one of the other great twists of fate in modern football, where Pochettino’s profile could be completely different. His Tottenham team were genuinely one of the best in Europe over 2016-18, and one of the great Premier League teams. To achieve 86 points in 2016-17, on what was then only the sixth highest wage bill in English football, was genuine alchemy. It was immense overperformance, fostered by a side that could just overrun you.

We also now know that the wage bill of the eventual champions for that season, Chelsea, had in part come from signings that had been secured by payments against the rules. The punishment from that guilty verdict still looks weak. There is a strong argument that Chelsea should have been stripped of the 2015 and 2017 titles. Pochettino himself said as much in a wide-ranging interview with The Independent and other media in September: “I’ve said that, that we should win one title, one Premier League. We should have been awarded it… for sure, we deserve to be champions for that year.”

Had that justice been done, Pochettino would not just be a “name” who created an exciting Spurs once. He would be an English champion, and one responsible for one of the most historic titles given the much wealthier competition. A great institution would have won just their third title, and first in 56 years.

Both he and Spurs could have had their futures transformed, as well as their place in history. It would have been a modern equivalent of what Ferguson himself did with Aberdeen.

Now, he wants to follow Ferguson in a different way. This is the job he has been waiting for.

A certain apathy towards the US job was displayed in that September interview when he spoke about how his contract didn’t necessarily mean he’d stay the full term.

For all of that, and how their World Cup campaign ended in the chaos of Donald Trump’s disruptive interference in the Falorin Balogun case, there were very impressive spells when the US really looked like a classic Pochettino team. The way they ripped into Paraguay was reminiscent of Spurs 2016-18, right up to some of the flourishes. And that was in a much more limited and restricted environment than a club team.

This is the other thing about just taking the job, too. Regardless of United’s current problems, and perceptions of where Pochettino is in his career, he is energised by this. He has that bite. As one figure who knows him well says, “he has got the IP, he has got the brand, he has got the experience”.

Having already worked for Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain, he’s been at big clubs with demanding owners. He has the mettle for that. And he now looks set to have the big job he’s always wanted.

#1041. Kane bends game to his will on record-breaking night

One day it will have to end for Harry Kane, but for now, almost 12 years into his England life, there is still no matching the wisdom and influence he has accumulated over all those games and all those goals for his country.

This would have been a great night by any measure for a man collecting his record-breaking 126th England cap. There was a handshake from Peter Shilton, now deposed as king of caps, and a flourish by Kane of his recently acquired Ballon d’Or, once his four children had accompanied him on to the pitch. These are the nights of which dreams are made, and yet – given the defining feature of Kane’s career – there was one more thing to accomplish.

That was, of course, a goal from the man who has ploughed relentlessly past the two great England individual landmarks of caps and goals. His second-half penalty won the game and, although he is not infallible from the spot, he is as close to that status as England have ever had. Age has not yet run him down, the game can still be bent to his will, and when it comes to the pressure moments, his longevity seems to offer the upper hand.

This was always going to be Kane’s night, with a great tifo on the west side of the stadium paying tribute to the England captain. The Prince of Wales was in attendance for the occasion, too. Luka Modric presented his former Tottenham Hotspur team-mate with a keepsake from the Croatian football federation. Kane had to wait for the second half for the most valuable offering of all.

After the hour, the Danish referee Morten Krogh was advised by his VAR Bastian Dankert to take a second look at a corner tangle involving Jarell Quansah, and decided to award the second-half penalty from which Kane scored. It was certainly clumsy, but these grapples have been overlooked by referees in the past. The 27th successfully converted penalty of the Kane England era followed, and the man himself played the full game.

Afterwards, Kane made a point of thanking the Football Association for organising it all, although it was also clear that this was no less than he expected. “It’s important to recognise the great players,” he said, “and it’s not something we have always done over the years.”

If the sentiment was a little awkwardly articulated, he is certainly right on the key point: so many England careers have ended abruptly at tournament elimination or elsewhere. Yet here was one being celebrated with the man himself in what might even be argued to his prime. Kane, 33, was asked again as to how long he might continue and did not rule out going on to 40, “if I’m performing at the highest level”.

That was a nod to Modric, a second-half substitute at the age of 41 and now on 207 caps for Croatia and almost 1,300 senior games. This Croatia team still seem unable to part company with their greatest player, despite his struggles against England in the seven-goal defeat in Rijeka. On this occasion, Croatia were much better.

It should have been more straightforward for England. They had taken the lead through Morgan Rogers midway through the first half and had dominated the first hour. But Quansah’s mistake gave Croatia an equaliser, and after Kane’s penalty England were fortunate to survive on occasions.

Alexander-Arnold gives the ball away in a dangerous position and Croatia combine for a crossing opportunity, but Hall is there at the back post to clear.

That is the final action of a rather uneventful first half, with Rogers’ strike from close range the difference at the break.

Baturina works room for a shot from the edge of the area but it’s comfortable again for Pickford, whose main scare this evening came when trying to play out from the back in the early minutes of the match.

Vlasic then wins a corner down Croatia’s left, with Rice tracking the run of the winger to block his cross. Bellingham heads marginally clear, though, before Hall completes the job.

England get to the edge of the Croatia box with some slick one-touch passing, but Alexander Arnold’s strike sails harmlessly over.

Elsewhere in this group, Spain have taken the lead against Czech Republic, taking them up to five wins from five as things stand.

England enjoy a lengthy spell of comfortable possession – they have had surprisingly few of those this evening.

Kane rakes another pass out to the right flank, but it’s marginally overhit this time.

Croatia work a free-kick short before sending it into the box towards Gvardiol but England manage to clear.

Moments later and Bellingham pinches it high up the pitch. He combines with Rogers and is fed into the right of the area but his low strike is blocked.

The Real Madrid man’s assist tonight means he has registered 14 goal involvements in his last 13 England games.

The Croatian coaching staff have been hugely impressed by the development of Morgan Rogers and talked about it before the game - with several of them, led by Slaven Bilic, having worked with him at West Bromwich Albion, Rogers’ first club.

Still they would have hoped to have defended better to prevent him from scoring so easily.

Croatia put together a slick move to beat the England press and it ends with a strike from range from Kovacic, but it’s straight down the throat of Pickford.

England are coming back for more, with Gordon fed into the left channel by Rice. The winger picks out former Newcastle team-mate Hall, making an underlapping run into the area, but his effort is blocked and behind for a corner.

Rice sends the set-piece towards the back post and Burn does all he can to get on the end of it but his header is blocked. England keep the pressure on, with the ball sent back into the area towards Burn, but the centre-back is penalised this time.

Once again we saw the importance of Harry Kane with that goal with the switch of play across goal to Jude Bellingham who teed up Morgan Rogers.

The backspin Kane put on his pass was superb as it delivered the ball precisely to Bellingham. It highlighted Kane’s passing range, a real feature of his game that marks him out from other centre-forwards.

England 1 Croatia 0 (Rogers) It’s not the prettiest goal but England are ahead.

Kane drops deep and plays a wonderful ball over the top to Bellingham in the right of the area.

The midfielder lays the ball square, and, after squirming through the legs of a couple of defenders, it’s stabbed home by Rogers from close range.

Gvardiol, in particular, could and should have done more there, but Tuchel will not care!

Alexander-Arnold proving his worth to the team in the last few minutes.

I was here the night England lost to Croatia in Nov 2007. They only had to draw that game to qualify for Euro 2008 and had already had a major stroke of luck with results elsewhere.

What I will say is no-one realised what a good Croatia team that would turn out to be and England had dreadful luck with injuries. If Darren Bent had buried that late chance the history of the national team would be very different. No Michael Owen, Wayne Rooney, John Terry. Wayne Bridge played despite illness. Even so, terrible night.

The visitors then nearly get caught out as they look to play in their own area, but the goalkeeper keeps his composure to find a way out.

This has been a concerning start from England. They look to play out from the back but Pickford nearly gets caught out and is forced to squirm the ball behind for another corner.

England manage to clear but Croatia are able to establish comfortable possession once again. A completely different feel to the reverse fixture.

Vlasic wins a corner down Croatia’s left, with Alexander-Anrold blocking the winger’s cross.

It’s a poor set-piece, though, allowing Kane to bring it away at the near post.

It’s Alexander-Arnold’s turn to give it away and Croatia look to break down their left but England get numbers back and force the visitors to recycle possession.

England win it back as Croatia build, but once again, England give it away in their own half. It’s been a sloppy start from the hosts.

There’s a few empty seats inside Wembley for Harry Kane’s big night. The Croatia corner, however, is packed out and it’s the visiting fans who have been louder so far.

It’s a nervy start from England, with Hall robbed in his own half and Anderson not convincing as he looks to deal with a cross into the box from Croatia’s right, but the ball deflects behind for a goal-kick.

We are underway at Wembley, with Croatia kicking things off, going from left to right in the opening period.

The national anthems are underway and kick-off will be next!

Kane leads his side out, with his children beside him. The Ballon d’Or is carried behind him, placed on a plinth and he steps away from his team-mates to present it to the Wembley crowd.

Luka Modric then gifts Kane with a present from Croatia, before Prince William hands him a framed England shirt, with “Kane 126” on the back.

Roy Hodgson, who gave him his first cap, is in the crowd applauding.

Thomas Tuchel has said he has “unfinished business” with England and will remain in his position for the Euros in 2028, but did say that he would return to club football after seeing out his contract.

“I signed the contract, I want to stay until the Euros,” he said this week. “I want to do the Euros. We have unfinished business.”

But he added: “I miss the 50 matches [a season].

“I miss the two minutes when everything is done. You go out two minutes before the whistle goes, it’s like the best two minutes, everything is done and you’re in a full stadium, lights are on and you’re just so excited and you’re part of it.”

This fixture is synonymous with one game in particular. It’s incredible to think it is nine days short of the 19th anniversary of England 2 Croatia 3, Steve McClaren’s ill-advised carrying umbrella, Slaven Bilic jumping around in the rain in a beany hat and David Beckham – then of LA Galaxy – finding himself starting amongst the substitutes as England failed to qualify for Euro 2008.

This observer was in the press box that evening, along with all the others contributing to this blog, and don’t we all feel old watching Rio Ngumoha, who was only a twinkle in the eyes of his parents, go through his warm up tonight.

Shortly before kick-off, Croatia captain Luka Modric will present England captain Harry Kane with a special gift from the Croatian Football Federation (HNS), marking his Ballon d’Or win and his achievement in becoming England’s all-time record appearance holder with 126 caps.

Modric is not in the starting line-up but the 41-year-old has 206 caps for his country and will present Kane with a specially crafted replica of the first football ever brought to Croatia, which English industrialists introduced to the town of Zupanja in 1880. This event is regarded as the beginning of organised football on Croatian soil.

England’s 3-0 home victory over Czech Republic last month left them on nine points after four Nations League group games.

It came after a 2-0 win in the away contest, a 7-0 thumping of Croatia and a 3-2 defeat against world champions Spain.

A draw tonight will be enough for Thomas Tuchel’s side to book their place in the quarter-finals of the competition.

The eight teams to finish in the top two of the four League A groups will play in the knockout rounds that start in March 2027.

The two worst sides to finish bottom are automatically relegated, while the other bottom sides and third-placed sides are at risk of relegation via a play-off.

Few expect Jobe to be better than his older brother. While Jobe will make his England debut just two months after turning 21, Jude’s first cap came aged 17. By the time that he was Jobe’s age now, Jude had already thrived for England in two international tournaments. But Jobe has one major sporting advantage: he is the younger sibling.

Younger siblings have significantly more chance of becoming elite athletes. If two siblings both become professional, the little sibling is significantly more likely to enjoy the better career.

Jude and Jobe Bellingham could become the first brothers to start for England since Gary and Phil Neville took to the field together 19 years ago, with Jobe included in his first senior squad.

Jack and Bobby Charlton are the only other brothers to play together for England in the post-war period.

“I can’t ignore it, but obviously with Jude being here too, it’s a great, great feeling for the family,” Jobe said on the FA’s England app as he discussed his call-up.

“It’s quite special, to be honest. It’s such a huge bonus on top of something that’s already so special and so great. To be called up for England is a dream itself and I’ve been so proud to have the opportunity to represent England at every age group.

“I always enjoyed coming away with England, I love competing against top players at whichever age group. But to have that chance of an opportunity to represent England with my brother, it’s really hard to put into words.

“I don’t have the words, really. I think it’s only emotion that could describe it, and, hopefully, if that time does come, you’ll see a lot of emotion from people, and definitely from my family.”

There will be a special pre-match presentation to honour Harry Kane becoming England’s record appearance maker, with 126 caps, overtaking Peter Shilton. Shilton has held the record since 1989.

The goalkeeper is at Wembley to formally mark Kane’s achievement. The England captain will also show the Ballon d’Or trophy he won last month.

Harry Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph from last month will also be celebrated tonight before kick-off, along with his record appearance.

“I think I maybe underappreciated how big it was going to be, how big the reaction was going to be,” he told the BBC.

“It’s just been crazy, whether it’s messages on my phone or on social media, or people calling me, and just being in the street and everyone congratulating me.

“I think the actual moment when Ronaldo said my name, it’s strange, it’s almost like a movie.

“In the moment, it was like in slow motion and the confetti was supposed to fall and all this, but when I watched it back, I had my hand to my mouth and maybe a couple of seconds and I was out, but in the actual moment, it felt like I was doing it for a minute.

“It was a really unique feeling because it is different to playing a game or scoring a goal, because it is so individual, it is nothing you can kind of do.

“Your mind is playing games with you the whole night, whether it is going to be you or not.

“So, when he actually said my name, it was just a crazy emotion.”

To the exclusive club of Billy Wright, Sir Bobby Charlton, Bobby Moore and Peter Shilton, the name Harry Kane will be added on Thursday night. It is only the fifth time that a new men’s England international appearance record has been set in the post-war era, with Kane preparing for his 126th England match to surpass a landmark that has stood for 36 years.

“I’ll be the first to congratulate him because I think he’s done it the right way,” says Shilton, who will be back at Wembley to metaphorically pass on the baton.

“He’s not coming on as a substitute; he’s been out there every game, doing his job. Records are there to be beaten and I couldn’t think of anybody better than Harry, not just on the pitch but off the pitch. I am very proud of the record and handing it to Harry makes it not quite as bad.

“I think striker is the hardest position to play and goalkeeper is the second hardest because of the responsibility you’ve got. But scoring goals is the most difficult thing and Harry’s record in the modern game is there to be seen.”

Thomas Tuchel has said Harry Kane was the deserved winner of the Ballon d’Or, with the England head coach describing the striker as “an extraordinary player”.

“He wins the Ballon d’Or, and deservedly so, and in the next game for England he gets the all-time record with 126 matches,” Tuchel said when announcing the latest squad.

“Thursday is a deserved occasion to celebrate an extraordinary player.”

Kane said: “It’s not about me – it’s about the team. I love coming to every England camp. I love playing every game and representing the country in the best way possible.”

Harry Kane starts for England in what will be a record 126th appearance for his country.

Thomas Tuchel makes three changes from last month’s win over Czech Republic, with Dan Burn, Declan Rice and Anthony Gordon replacing Marc Guehi, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Eberechi Eze.

Harry Kane will become England’s record appearance maker this evening, with the 33-year-old set to earn his 126th cap.

The striker started his international career against Lithuania in March 2015, scoring just 79 second after replacing Wayne Rooney at Wembley.

Eight years later, Kane surpassed Rooney as the country’s record goalscorer, netting his 54th England goal in an away contest with Italy.

He equalled Peter Shilton’s record of 125 caps last month against Czech Republic as he scored his 90th and 91st international goals.

England will be hoping for a repeat of their fixture against Croatia last month, with Thomas Tuchel’s side producing an emphatic 7-0 victory in Rijeka.

England were 4-0 up at half-time of the Nations League contest, which was attended by 6,000 schoolchildren and 100 visiting fans, with Croatia supporters sanctioned over previous bad behaviour.

England’s front four of Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Bukayo Saka were all on the scoresheet in the opening period, with Kane and Saka doubling their tallies in the second half before a late seventh from Morgan Rogers.

Good evening and welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of England vs Croatia in the Nations League, with the hosts’ captain Harry Kane set to become the country’s most-capped player.

The 33-year-old has enjoyed a memorable few weeks, becoming the first English Ballon d’Or winner in 25 years and following it up with a new Bayern Munich contract, and an appearance at Wembley tonight will take him clear of Peter Shilton’s record of 125 England caps.

Kane scored twice in his record-equalling appearance against Czech Republic at Wembley last month, extending his international tally to 91 goals – a total that is unrivalled for England.

“It’s not about me – it’s about the team,” Kane said before tonight’s landmark moment. “I love coming to every England camp. I love playing every game and representing the country in the best way possible.”

The 3-0 home victory over Czech Republic left England on nine points after four Nations League group games, with a 2-0 win in the away contest and a 7-0 thumping of Croatia coming after a 3-2 defeat against world champions Spain.

Thomas Tuchel will be hoping that his side can inflict another heavy defeat on Croatia this evening, but a draw will be enough to book their place in the quarter-finals, with the group’s top two teams progressing.

While Kane will collect plaudits for his 126th cap, attention will also be on a potential first, with Jude Bellingham’s younger brother, Jobe, included in a senior England squad for the first time.

The two Bellinghams appearing together in a senior match would be a new experience for them, while it would be the first time that brothers have taken to the field together for England in 19 years.

“I can’t ignore it, but obviously with Jude being here too, it’s a great, great feeling for the family,” Jobe said on the Football Association’s England app. “It’s quite special, to be honest. It’s such a huge bonus on top of something that’s already so special and so great.”

Michael Carrick has been sacked as Manchester United manager after overseeing the club’s worst start to the Premier League season in 40 years, with Mauricio Pochettino looking set to replace him.

A second Old Trafford comeback of the week, this time battling from two goals down twice to rescue a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday, was not enough to save Carrick’s job and the club announced on Thursday that it had parted ways with him after just 10 games of the season and with his side 18th during the international break.

United ended a nine-game winless run when they came from two goals down to beat Roma in the Champions League last week but they have not won in eight attempts in the Premier League and have just one top-flight win this campaign.

Carrick survived crisis talks with the United hierarchy after defeats to Como and Bournemouth last month and was given time to turn results around, but speculation over a change begun the day after Sunday’s chaotic draw and The Independent understands contact was initially made with United States boss Pochettino over succeeding Carrick on Monday.

The Old Trafford hierarchy, including Jason Wilcox, Omar Berrarda and Sir Jim Ratcliffe, met in Monaco to discuss Carrick’s future and the club are on the verge of hashing out a deal with Pochettino, who is reportedly ready to accept the position.

Follow latest updates from Old Trafford here:

Pep Guardiola is a “top target” to become the next USA head coach with Mauricio Pochettino set to leave the role and become Manchester United manager.

Michael Carrick was finally sacked by United on Thursday morning and, as The Independent first reported a few days ago, Pochettino is being lined up for a return to club football to take over at Old Trafford.

The deal is currently being finalised, with an official announcement expected relatively soon, although the specifics of when exactly the Argentine will leave his USMNT role is not yet clear, with a two-legged Concacaf Nations League quarter-final clash against Haiti taking place on Saturday and Tuesday.

Man United could break the £100m barrier for spending on hiring and firing managers since Sir Alex Ferguson’s exit in 2013.

Punchy stuff from Sky Sports reporter Geoff Shreeves.

Harry Maguire has taken to Instagram to pay tribute to Michael Carrick following his Man United sacking, thanking his now former manager.

Manchester United are working to finalise a deal to appoint United States head coach Mauricio Pochettino after sacking Michael Carrick.

A framework had already been established for the former Argentina international’s appointment, with talks understood to be progressing between the Old Trafford club and Pochettino’s employers US Soccer.

United’s next fixture is against Liverpool in the Premier League before a run of games against clubs that could firmly place them in a relegation battle should they fail to win them.

Liverpool (A) - Premier League - Sunday November 22

Sporting (A) - Champions League - Wednesday November 25

Brentford (H) - Premier League - Saturday November 28

Newcastle (A) - Premier League - Wednesday December 2

Coventry (H) - Premier League - Saturday December 5

RB Leipzig (H) - Champions League - Tuesday December 8

The Manchester United Supporters’ Trust (MUST) has branded Michael Carrick’s sacking “another depressing moment” and argued the club’s problems rest primarily with its ownership, in a now-familiar plea to end the ongoing feeling of crisis at Old Trafford.

United sacked Carrick just 10 games into the Premier League season with the club in the relegation zone and having won just once in this domestic campaign.

The club’s hierarchy met minority owner Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco on Wednesday to discuss Carrick’s future and a statement on Thursday said that it had “come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions”.

Paul Scholes thinks Man United might be going in for Mauricio Pochettino a few years too late.

He said on The Good, The Bad & The Football, in partnership with Midnite: “I love Pochettino and we work with him at Soccer Aid, didn’t we, he’s a he’s a great man. I think he’s got the presence to manage a big football club like Manchester United.

“He’s got the respect to do it. He works with young players which obviously Manchester United want. My only slight concern is have that we come a little bit too late to the party.

“I think we’ve done that in the past. You look at Van Gaal, his best years were probably behind him. Mourinho again, I think his best years were probably behind him. Saying that, I’m not ruling out what he’s going to do with this Real Madrid team because this Real Madrid team look good.

“I just - when you really think about when we was talking about this two or three weeks ago after the Bournemouth game I don’t think any of us mentioned Pochettino.”

Today is only the sixth time in Premier League history two managers - Michael Carrick and Pierre Sage - have left their positions on the same day during a season.

The last time it happened actually wasn’t that long ago, with Wolves boss Gary O'Neil and Southampton manager Russell Martin both getting canned on 15 December 2024.

Pochettino is still contracted to US Soccer until the 2030 World Cup though an early departure from his deal feels increasingly likely. United have made contact with US Soccer over paying compensation to release Pochettino with rumoured figures reaching as high a $10m (£7.4m).

Should an agreement be made, Pochettino could, in theory, leave the US before the scheduled games against Haiti in order to spend time with Man United’s squad ahead of the crucial clash at Anfield.

In that case he could arrive at Carrington either the same day or a day after being formally announced as the new head coach. That would give him a maximum of nine days to prepare the team if his appointment is confirmed today (Thursday 12 November).

The more likelier option is that Pochettino leads the USMNT for their two fixtures with Haiti and reports to Carrington shortly afterwards.

In that case, he could be in post at Man United as early as Wednesday 18 November though given the time difference between the US and the UK, Pochettino would arrive late in the afternoon or early evening.

Even so, that would give him three full days, Thursday 19, Friday 20 and Saturday 21 to settle into his new environment and have time on the grass with the squad.

Beau Greaves says she is "excited" to face Luke Littler on the opening day of the Grand Slam of Darts this weekend.

Greaves has been drawn in the same group as Littler and Dutch player Niels Zonneveld with only the top player from each group progressing to the knockout stages.

Littler and Greaves will meet for the first time since the latter beat the world champion at the World Youth Championship 12 months ago in Saturday's night's Grand Slam of Darts session, which begins at 7pm, live on Sky Sports.

"I think he's the best [player in the world] in my eyes, I think he's fantastic to watch, he's been amazing, so I always imagine he's going to play really well," said Greaves.

"I don't want to go in there thinking, 'oh he's not on form', or he's struggling, because then I would just be terrible, so I've got to go in there thinking 'he's going to absolutely smash me', and just play my game, and try and take any chance I can, and just enjoy it.

"I think it's going to be a good game just to watch, and just to be a part of it is special. I look forward to playing it."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Greaves has played in the last three Grand Slam of Darts and won two matches but is yet to get out of the group stages.

The 22-year-old narrowly lost to Michael van Gerwen and Gary Anderson, despite averaging over 100, last year and is hoping to perform well on the big stage once again.

"I played decent at the Grand Slam last year. I have good moments, but I just don't do it consistently enough," she said.

"It's something that, if I am going to do really well in the sport, I'm going to have to get better at. It's a challenge for me, but I look forward to it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I always look forward to kind of getting better and improving. I'm aware that obviously I'm not up to that standard as I do play on the floor, but it's just a work in progress at the minute, I would call it.

"But I'm just trying to look forward to everything rather than dread anything and obviously look forward to playing on stage rather than think I'd rather play on the floor. So, I'm just trying to switch it around a little bit."

The Grand Slam has expanded this year from 32 to 48 players and sees 16 groups of three, rather than four players in a group.

The format adds jeopardy as anybody who loses their opening match will be under serious pressure and could be eliminated, even if they win their second match.

"I didn't know. I didn't have a clue that there was only three in the group! I don't know why they've done it really. It didn't make much sense to me, but again, I don't really know," said Greaves.

"It's just odd, but I suppose you've still got to do well to win your group regardless but it's different, I was a bit shocked."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Greaves says she has felt "relaxed" when playing Littler in the past and is "excited" to face the world No 1, who has won the last two Grand Slam of Darts titles.

"I know Luke's loads better than me, but I kind of have to at least convince myself I can win," she said.

"I can't go up there wanting to get beat but I know it's obviously, he's 10 times better than me, but strange to think about if you get beat.

"Luke Littler is the heavy favourite to come through that group obviously, so it's strange, but there is a big jump in prize money if you finish second or third, so there's still a little bit to play for on the ranking, so just trying to not think about it and just try and enjoy every game, and try and do my best."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Also speaking to media on Thursday was Ross Smith, two weeks on from his European Championship title success.

Smith joined Michael van Gerwen, Phil Taylor, Rob Cross and Peter Wright as a multiple winner of the European Championship, following his 2022 success by defeating Martin Schindler 11-8 in the final in Dortmund.

The Englishman's latest triumph adds to his World Series Finals victory in September and sees him rise to a career-high sixth in the PDC Order of Merit.

"I've already proved I have the game to beat the best," Smith said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I have beaten Luke Littler, I have beaten Luke Humphries. Maybe not at a major event or anything, but I can only play the players I'm drawn against.

"But I'm definitely not afraid of playing them, that's for sure. And I actually relish and look forward to it.

"It's just about knuckling down and getting the wins. Whoever's in front of me, I don't really think about both the Lukes or anyone else. It's just the person in front of me. That's all I can do."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Smith was speaking a day after PDC chief executive Matt Porter told Sky Sports the 37-year-old was now "one of the best players in the world" and firmly in his thinking for the 2027 Premier League.

Asked for his response, Smith said: "I read it this morning. It's always nice to get credit for when you're playing well, especially from the top end of the game and the guys sitting there making the decisions. It's great to hear.

"Again, I'll just wait for the phone call or message or email, whatever it is. It's just nice to get the recognition that all the hard work is paying off at the moment.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I'm not going to even read into it. A few years ago when I won the Euros, I put too much pressure on myself. I don't think I've really got anything to prove.

"I've beaten every single player out there - I've also been beaten by most of them as well. It's out of my hands regardless.

"I'm just trying to embrace everything and the opportunity that's been given to me. Of course I want to be in the Premier League. I should be in it, but again, that's not my call.

"At the same time, I'm grateful to be where I am. I've got an amazing job, something that I always wanted as a kid. I've got amazing family and friends around me. What more do I want in life, you know? I'm just happy in life."

The Frenchman departs after a fourth consecutive Premier League defeat and with the Eagles bottom of the table

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Crystal Palace have sacked manager Pierre Sage after the club slumped to bottom of the Premier League table for the first time since December 2017.

The Frenchman moved to Selhurst Park on a three-year contract this summer after an impressive year at Lens, where he led the club to a runner-up finish in Ligue 1, won the Coupe de France and Trophee des Champions titles for the first time, and qualified for the Champions League.

But he was unable to replicate that success across his 16 games in all competitions at Palace, who have conceded the most goals of any top-flight side this season and claimed just seven points out of a possible 30 during his tenure, and sit two points off safety going into the November international break.

A club statement released on Thursday said: “Crystal Palace Football Club can confirm that Pierre Sage has left his role as Manager.

“The club would like to place on record its thanks to Pierre and his staff for their efforts during their time in South London, and wish them well for the future.

“An update on the process of appointing a new Manager will be provided in due course.”

Former Brentford and Tottenham manager Thomas Frank could be considered as Palace now attempt to rescue themselves from a relegation fight, while former Burnley, Everton and Nottingham Forest boss Sean Dyche is also out of work and would be available.

Three members of Sage’s coaching staff, Jamal Alioui, Damien Della Santa and Sandy Guichard, have also departed.

Sage leaves after a 3-1 defeat to Liverpool at Selhurst Park, which marked Palace’s fourth straight league loss and seventh in the top-flight this season. Palace also have one win, two draws and one defeat from four Europa League games and are through to the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup, where they play Sunderland next month.

The former Lyon boss had replaced perhaps the most successful Crystal Palace manager in modern history in Oliver Glasner, who won the FA Cup and Conference League with the Eagles before moving to Premier League rivals Nottingham Forest at the end of last season.

#1036. DeepMind’s ultra-powerful AI for genome mapping wows scientists

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

In 2024, researchers found a new driver of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD): it was a gene called ETS2 that is overactive in immune cells owing to a DNA variant that predisposes people to the condition1. This variant had previously confounded researchers because it lies in a ‘gene desert’ nowhere near protein-coding sequences.

That discovery had involved gene-editing and other sophisticated molecular-biology techniques, and it identified potential new IBD treatments. Now, researchers at Google DeepMind in London have replicated aspects of the finding using an artificial-intelligence model, and they have done this without lifting a pipette. Their model is called AlphaGenome 2.

“They’ve managed to figure out the answer in 30 minutes, and it took us a year and a half of experiments,” says James Lee, an immunologist and geneticist at the Francis Crick Institute in London who led the 2024 study. “It’s reassuring from our perspective.”

The AlphaGenome 2 model, which was announced today, is an update to an AI tool that predicts the molecular effects that ‘non-coding’ DNA sequences have, such as on the expression of other genes. These sequences comprise 98% of the human genome, but they are among the hardest to decipher. The latest model makes these predictions in hundreds of mouse and human cell types.

Two months ago, Google DeepMind released the AlphaGenome Atlas: these were predictions for every possible single-letter DNA change to the human genome — a total of nine billion variants.

These and other predictions were made with a tool called AlphaGenome 1 and came with a major caveat: they did not specify the precise kind of cell — be it antibody-making B cells or pancreatic β-cells — in which a variant was likely to act. “Having something that cannot predict cell-type specificity is a bit of a problem, which is why it hasn’t been hugely useful for us,” says Lee.

But researchers know that many non-coding DNA sequences — including the variant that Lee’s team mapped, which is part of a sequence called a gene enhancer — tend to be active in specific types of cell.

“If you want to understand variants associated with genetic diseases, then you have to ask yourself what are the cell types that are affected,” says Žiga Avsec, a DeepMind researcher who leads the AlphaGenome team.

To develop an AI model that could decipher variant effects in diverse cells, Avsec’s team trained AlphaGenome 2 on single-cell gene activity and other measurements made in more than 100 million cells, across 68 tissues. AlphaGenome 1, by contrast, was fed data collected in ‘bulk’ samples of heterogeneous cells.

The result is a richer, more fine-grained representation of the differences between cells, says Adam Gayoso, a Google DeepMind scientist and co-author of a preprint describing the model on the company’s website.

AlphaGenome 2 also isn’t limited to making predictions in the 637 types of human cell and 311 kinds of mouse cell it was trained on. Researchers can provide the model with new single-cell gene-activity data — such as those from cells in a disease state — and generate gene-variant predictions. This could help researchers to identify variants underlying disease more quickly, says Gayoso.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03673-0

Stankey, C. T. et al. Nature 630, 447–456 (2024).

Named after Diego Maradona, Diego Demme helped Napoli win their first Scudetto in the post-Maradona era

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Few players have transformed a club as Diego Maradona did for Napoli. After winning two trophies in their first six decades, Napoli won five in six seasons with Maradona. Maradona's face still adorns the city walls today, and his legacy is etched into the hearts of Napoli supporters like Enzo Demme.

Enzo was seven when he left Italy for Germany, carving out a playing career that took him as high as the 3. Bundesliga. Despite living in Germany, he never stopped supporting Napoli or idolizing Maradona. Even as he was serving a 15-month suspension for cocaine, Demme paid homage to Maradona by naming his son Diego.

Diego followed in Enzo's footballing footsteps with Arminia Bielefeld and Paderborn before spurring RB Leipzig from the third tier to the Champions League. However, silverware eluded the Leipzig captain, whose closest brush with glory ended in defeat to Bayern Munich in the 2018/19 DFB-Pokal Final.

With Leipzig sitting atop the Bundesliga and challenging for their maiden championship, Demme made the surprising decision to join a Napoli side in crisis in January 2020. He established himself as a midfield linchpin, winning the 2019/20 Coppa Italia and ending their six-year trophy drought.

After claiming their fourth trophy of the post-Maradona era, Demme helped Napoli go from seventh to fifth to third to first in Serie A, winning the 2022/23 Scudetto with five games remaining. Unlike in 2020, when COVID-19 restrictions kept supporters apart, Napoli fans could finally take to the streets and celebrate their team's triumph together.

"We won at Udinese and flew back to Napoli, and the whole airport was closed because there were too many people at the airport," stated Demme in an exclusive FourFourTwo interview. "We went to the military airport, and there were still so many people."

Napoli fans had spent 33 years wondering whether the sun would shine on them again after Maradona. 30 months after Maradona's untimely passing, they had finally found their answer.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"I can't explain the sensation of winning the Scudetto, because it was unbelievable. We were driving from the airport, and behind the bus, there were 200 scooters in the tunnel. They were next to each other, and there was no space, and everybody was celebrating. I was like, ‘Wow, if something happens, then there will be a domino effect, and everyone will fall."

For Enzo, it was the culmination of a lifelong love affair with Napoli. Having watched from afar as Maradona inspired their first Scudetti in 1987 and 1990, he could finally celebrate the title in Naples alongside the son he'd named after his footballing hero.

"My father was crying because it was so emotional for him, because of the whole Maradona story and the Scudetto," added Demme. "Today, when I see the pictures, I think of how wonderful it was. It was a crazy night. We were celebrating with the whole city, and it was great."

Diego Demme, in Herford geboren, hat seinen Vornamen, weil sein Vater Maradona- und Napoli-Fan ist. Schon beim Wechsel aus Leipzig zur SSC Neapel war ein bisschen Familienromantik dabei. Jetzt dürfte Vater Enzo stolz wie Bolle sein. https://t.co/Pq1gHNn7u0May 5, 2023

For a man who had spent nearly his entire life away from Italy, it was a poignant homecoming. The seven-year-old boy who had carried his adoration for Napoli across the Alps had lived long enough to see his son restore his team to the promised land.

Demme left the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona in 2024, spending two years at Hertha Berlin before retiring last month. He's still keeping his Napoli roots alive as the co-owner of two Neapolitan pizzerias in Berlin, and he plans to open another in Tbilisi with ex-teammate Khvicha Kvaratshkelia.

Three decades after being named after Napoli's greatest hero, Diego Demme has come full circle. Football brought him back to his father's homeland, and even after hanging up his boots, he's ensuring that a slice of Naples will always remain with him.
